docs.title: Language of this site
docs.text:
This site is written in English. Some posts are in Dutch, because they are about the Netherlands: Dutch policy, Dutch regulators, Dutch institutions and Dutch places. The reason is practical rather than principled. An English text on such a subject fills up with Dutch names, terms and document titles that have no natural English equivalent, and then it reads worse than the original would have. Everything that is not about the Netherlands stays in English.

Die uitzondering staat er bewust: berichten die primair over Nederland gaan kunnen in het Nederlands staan, alle andere berichten zijn Engelstalig.

docs.title: Building a Markdown-Powered Website with MkDocs
docs.text:
As a Markdown enthusiast, I've grown accustomed to creating content using this versatile format. Recently, I set out to build a website that leverages Markdown's ease of use, allowing me to create pages with minimal fuss. My search led me to Static Site HTML generators, which sparked a chain reaction of discoveries: GitHub Pages, Jekyll, and eventually, MkDocs and MkDocs-Material. The latter's impressive capabilities had me hooked, and I wanted to take it to the next level by integrating Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) to automate the deployment process.

With this goal in mind, I embarked on a mission to create a seamless workflow, where changes to my Markdown files would trigger a build, followed by automatic deployment to a production environment. The thrill of the challenge was palpable, and I'm excited to share my journey with you.

docs.title: Het rijke verleden blootgelegd: een reis door de Nederlandse geschiedenis
docs.text: Nederland, een klein land met een reusachtige erfenis, heeft een geschiedenis die de eigen identiteit vormde én grote invloed had op de rest van de wereld. Van prehistorische nederzettingen tot een wereldwijd handelsimperium en een moderne democratie: in vogelvlucht langs de tijdperken die dit fascinerende land hebben gevormd.

docs.title: Prehistorie (voor 500 v.Chr.)
docs.text: Lang voordat kanalen het landschap doorkruisten en molens de horizon sierden, woonden er al vroege menselijke bewoners in Nederland. Aanwijzingen duiden op menselijke aanwezigheid uit het paleolithicum, rond 250.000 v.Chr. Stel je vroege stammen voor die door de uitgestrekte moerassen en dichte bossen trokken, met de machtige Rijn-Maasdelta als natuurlijke wieg van de vroegst bekende nederzettingen. Dit was het domein van verschillende stammen, waaronder de later gedocumenteerde Bataven, Cananefaten en Friezen, die de basis legden voor de uiteenlopende regionale identiteiten die zouden ontstaan.

docs.title: Romeinse tijd (500 v.Chr. - 450 n.Chr.)
docs.text: De komst van de Romeinen in de 1e eeuw v.Chr. betekende een belangrijk keerpunt. Ze veroverden niet alleen; ze brachten organisatie, infrastructuur en een nieuwe manier van leven. Met de provincie Germania Inferior lieten de Romeinen een onuitwisbare indruk achter met hun wegen, versterkingen en nederzettingen. Denk aan Ulpia Noviomagus, het huidige Nijmegen, een bewijs van Romeinse stedenbouw. Dit tijdperk ging niet alleen over verovering; het was een periode van levendige handel en culturele uitwisseling, die deze noordelijke buitenpost verbond met het uitgestrekte Romeinse Rijk.

docs.title: Volksverhuizingstijd en vroege middeleeuwen (450 - 1000 n.Chr.)
docs.text: Toen het Romeinse Rijk zich terugtrok, golfde een nieuwe verandering over Nederland. Verschillende Germaanse stammen, met name de Franken en Saksen, trokken de regio binnen en hervormden de bevolkingsopbouw en het politieke landschap. De Franken bleken bijzonder invloedrijk: zij stichtten het Frankische Rijk, dat zich uiteindelijk zou ontwikkelen tot het machtige Heilige Roomse Rijk. In deze periode ontstonden ook de kloosters en de verspreiding van het christendom, die de geestelijke en intellectuele basis legden voor de eeuwen die volgden.

docs.title: Middeleeuwen (1000 - 1500 n.Chr.)
docs.text: In de middeleeuwen veranderde Nederland in een bruisend centrum van handel en commercie. De befaamde Hanze speelde een sleutelrol en verbond Nederlandse kooplieden met een uitgebreid netwerk in Noord-Europa. Politiek gezien was de regio een lappendeken van graafschappen en heerlijkheden, waarbij het graafschap Holland geleidelijk zijn overwicht als machtige eenheid liet gelden. Dit tijdperk liet ons ook blijvende tastbare erfenissen na: de majestueuze kastelen, kerken en kloosters die het landschap vandaag nog steeds sieren, fluisteringen van een levendig middeleeuws verleden.

docs.title: Gouden Eeuw (1500 - 1700 n.Chr.)
docs.text: Als er één periode is die echt schittert in de Nederlandse geschiedenis, dan is het de Gouden Eeuw. Het was een tijd van ongekende economische groei en culturele bloei. Nederland werd een onbetwist belangrijk centrum voor handel, financiën en kunst, met steden als Amsterdam en Leiden die bruisten van commercie en creativiteit. De oprichting van de Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie in 1602 was niet zomaar een bedrijfsgebeurtenis; zij luidde het begin in van een aanzienlijke koloniale periode, breidde de invloed van het land wereldwijd uit en bevestigde zijn reputatie als maritieme grootmacht.

docs.title: Moderne tijd (1700 - heden)
docs.text:
De reis eindigde niet met de Gouden Eeuw. Nederland bleef een belangrijke speler op het internationale toneel, droeg bij aan de Verlichting en omarmde de ingrijpende verschuivingen van de Industriële Revolutie. Het land maakte ingrijpende sociale en economische veranderingen door, zag de opkomst van een stevige middenklasse en, cruciaal, de afschaffing van de slavernij. Vandaag staat Nederland als een trotse, moderne, seculiere democratie. Het land is wereldwijd bekend om zijn tolerante samenleving, hoge levensstandaard en rijke culturele erfgoed, dat zich blijft ontwikkelen en diep geworteld is in de lagen van zijn fascinerende verleden.

docs.title: A fascinating topic in mathematics and art
docs.text:
Penrose tiles are a type of non-periodic tiling, named after the mathematician Roger Penrose, who first described them in the 1970s. These tiles are designed to fit together without any gaps or overlaps, but they cannot be repeated in a regular pattern.

Here are some interesting facts about Penrose tiles:

  1. Non-periodic: Penrose tiles are non-periodic, meaning that they cannot be repeated in a regular pattern. This is in contrast to traditional periodic tilings, such as brick walls or hexagonal tiles, which repeat in a predictable pattern.
  2. Aperiodic: Penrose tiles are also aperiodic, meaning that they do not have a repeating pattern. This is what makes them so unique and interesting.
  3. Two types of tiles: There are two types of Penrose tiles: the "Rhombus" and the "Kite". The Rhombus tile has two acute angles and two obtuse angles, while the Kite tile has two acute angles and two right angles.
  4. Tiling rules: To create a Penrose tiling, you need to follow specific rules. The Rhombus tile can be placed in one of two ways, and the Kite tile can be placed in one of four ways. These rules ensure that the tiles fit together without gaps or overlaps.
  5. Infinity: Penrose tilings can be extended infinitely in all directions, without repeating. This means that you can create a Penrose tiling that covers an entire surface, without ever repeating a pattern.
  6. Artistic applications: Penrose tilings have been used in various artistic applications, such as architecture, design, and even music. They add a unique and fascinating element to any design.
  7. Mathematical significance: Penrose tilings have significant mathematical implications. They demonstrate the existence of non-periodic structures and have connections to other areas of mathematics, such as group theory and algebraic geometry.

If you're interested in exploring Penrose tiles further, you can try creating your own tiling using paper or digital tools. There are also many online resources and software available to help you create and manipulate Penrose tilings.

docs.title: We are AI
docs.text: The concept of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is in an important sense a reflection of the choices humans make: systems are trained on material people produced, and they are optimised for goals people set. That inheritance shows up in measurable ways — in who a model gets wrong, and in what it asserts with complete confidence.

docs.title: Bias is inherited, and it can be measured
docs.text:
Three well-documented cases show what "the model reflects its training data" means in practice.

  • Recruiting. Amazon built an experimental system from 2014 to screen résumés and scrapped it after it taught itself that male candidates were preferable: it penalised résumés containing the word "women's" and downgraded graduates of two all-women's colleges, as Reuters reported in 2018.
  • Face analysis. The peer-reviewed Gender Shades study (Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018) tested three commercial gender-classification systems and found that darker-skinned women were misclassified in up to 34.7 percent of cases, against a maximum error rate of 0.8 percent for lighter-skinned men. MIT News reported the same disparity: error rates above 20 percent for darker-skinned women, never worse than 0.8 percent for light-skinned men.
  • Risk scores. ProPublica's 2016 analysis of the COMPAS recidivism tool found that it wrongly flagged Black defendants as future criminals at almost twice the rate of white defendants, while the overall error rate for both groups was roughly equal.

That the model amplifies what is already overrepresented in its training data is the argument of On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots (Bender, Gebru, McMillan-Major & Shmitchell, 2021): for US and UK English, the authors write, "white supremacist and misogynistic, ageist, etc. views are overrepresented in the training data", which sets models up to amplify those biases further.

docs.title: Fluent output is not understanding
docs.text: The same paper defines a language model as a system that stitches together sequences of linguistic forms "according to probabilistic information about how they combine, but without any reference to meaning". That is a narrower claim than saying a model lacks empathy — the sources reviewed for this post do not measure empathy, and the two should not be treated as the same thing. What is documented is that fluency and correctness are separate properties: a peer-reviewed survey of hallucination in natural language generation (Ji et al., ACM Computing Surveys, 2023) records that deep-learning text generation is "prone to hallucinate unintended text" that fails user expectations in real-world use. In a decision-support context — a risk score, a screening tool, a summary — that gap is where the risk sits.

docs.title: What is being built around it
docs.text:
Because these systems make consequential choices, the design requirements have moved from opinion to published rules:

  • Transparency. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework (2023) exists to incorporate "trustworthiness considerations into the design, development, use, and evaluation of AI products, services, and systems".
  • Disclosure. Article 50 of the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) obliges providers to ensure that people are informed when they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious from the context.
  • Interpretability. Article 13 of the same regulation requires high-risk systems to be designed so that their operation is "sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system's output and use it appropriately".

docs.title: The scale at which this matters
docs.text: These are no longer pilot projects. Stanford HAI's AI Index Report 2025 records that 78 percent of organisations reported using AI in 2024, up from 55 percent a year earlier — and adds that AI-related incidents are rising sharply while standardised responsible-AI evaluations "remain rare among major industrial model developers".

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• AI systems inherit human choices: the training data and the objective function are the design decision, and their effects are measurable (Gender Shades, COMPAS, Amazon's recruiting tool).
  • Fluency is not understanding; the documented failure mode is confident, plausible and wrong output (hallucination surveys), not "unfeeling" prose.
  • Transparency, disclosure and interpretability are now standards and legal requirements rather than preferences (NIST AI RMF; EU AI Act Articles 13 and 50).
  • Deployment has outrun evaluation: most organisations now use AI, while standardised testing of its risks lags behind.

docs.title: Updates van ABN-risicomodellen vertraagd
docs.text: ABN Amro heeft de verbetering van zijn risicomodellen uitgesteld. Daardoor houdt de bank op dit moment meer kapitaal aan dan nodig is. De vertraging schuift ook de beslissing over de aandeleninkoop op tot halverwege 2025. De bank worstelt al langer met de kwaliteit van haar risicomodellen en data, die niet volledig voldoen aan de eisen van de toezichthouder.

docs.title: Voortgang en uitdagingen
docs.text:
De bank heeft extra personeel aangenomen om haar risicomodellen en data te verbeteren, maar dat traject duurt langer dan verwacht. ABN Amro wil de invoering van de Basel IV-regels en de update van haar risicomodellen voor het einde van het tweede kwartaal van 2025 afronden. Pas daarna beslist de raad van bestuur of er ruimte is voor een aandeleninkoop.

CFO Ferdinand Vaandrager merkt op dat het vinden van geschikt talent met kennis van bankrisico's en regelgeving in Nederland een uitdaging is.

docs.title: Wisseling van de leiding en financiële resultaten
docs.text:
CEO Robert Swaak heeft aangekondigd dat hij in de eerste helft van 2025 vertrekt bij ABN Amro. De zoektocht naar zijn opvolger is al begonnen.

Ondanks deze uitdagingen boekte ABN Amro in het derde kwartaal een winst van 690 miljoen euro, een daling van 9% vergeleken met hetzelfde kwartaal een jaar eerder. De nettorente-inkomsten kwamen uit op 1,6 miljard euro en overtroffen de verwachtingen van analisten. De kosten-inkomstenratio was 59,2%, lager dan verwacht.

Robert Swaak blijft optimistisch over de toekomst. Hij wijst op de veerkracht van de Nederlandse economie en de bloeiende woningmarkt. Ook verwacht hij dat de Europese Centrale Bank de rente blijft verlagen, wat de bank ten goede zou komen.

docs.title: Chat control: the EU proposal to scan messages for abuse material
docs.text: On 11 May 2022, the European Commission presented a regulation to tackle child sexual abuse material online (COM(2022) 209). The proposal obliges online services to map out risks, gives authorities the power to have material removed or blocked, and sets up a European centre for coordination and victim support. Its most debated part are the detection orders: mandatory detection of abuse material in communications. Member states and the European Parliament do not yet agree on whether that power should exist, and with which safeguards.

docs.title: What the proposal covers
docs.text:
• Risk assessment. Providers of hosting services, messaging services and app stores must assess how their service could be used to spread abuse material or to approach children, and take measures against it.
  • Removal and blocking orders. National authorities can order a service to remove material or to block access to it.
  • A European centre. A new agency for coordination, expertise, research and victim support.
  • Detection orders. A judge or an independent authority can oblige a provider to search a specific service for known and new abuse material. This part touches on encrypted communication and on the confidentiality of communications, and is the most contested point in the debate.

docs.title: The temporary arrangement already in force
docs.text: Since 2021 a temporary exception to the European privacy rules for electronic communications (ePrivacy) has applied. It allows platforms to scan messages voluntarily; the exception was extended afterwards and is known in the debate as "chat control 1.0". The proposal is meant to replace it with a permanent framework, with requirements on accuracy, reporting and oversight.

docs.title: Where opinions diverge
docs.text:
Privacy and civil rights organisations, including EDRi, point to the consequences of scanning messages: pressure on end-to-end encryption, loss of anonymity in communication, and the risk that automatic detection marks files as abuse material when they are not, with consequences for the people affected. They argue for dropping the detection orders and for focusing on targeted detection by law enforcement.

On the other side stands the aim of the proposal: child protection organisations and the European Commission point to the volume of material circulating online and note that voluntary detection does not happen everywhere, so part of the material stays out of sight. In their reading, a common framework with independent oversight is more effective than the current patchwork of voluntary arrangements per platform.

To what extent detection works technically is part of the dispute. With automatic file comparison, outcomes depend on the technique used and on human review afterwards; figures on the number of findings and on the number of errors that follow from them are presented differently by different parties.

docs.title: What is still uncertain
docs.text:
• Whether the detection orders will remain in the final text, and if so, with which safeguards (judicial review, restriction to known files, exceptions).
  • How effectiveness will be measured and who reports on it.
  • When the negotiations between the European Parliament and the Council will be concluded. As long as there is no agreement, the proposal remains under consideration and the temporary arrangement stays in force.

docs.title: Import tariffs
docs.text: An import tariff is a tax levied on goods entering a country. It's essentially an additional cost added to the price of the imported product.

docs.title: How does an import tariff work?
docs.text:
Imagine a Dutch company imports shoes from China. The Dutch government might decide to impose an import tariff of, for example, 10% on shoes. This means that for every shoe the Dutch company imports, they have to pay an extra 10% of the shoe's value to the Dutch government.

There are different ways an import tariff can be levied:

  • Ad valorem tariff: This is the most common type of tariff and is expressed as a percentage of the customs value of the goods. In the example above, the 10% tariff is an ad valorem tariff.
  • Specific tariff: This is a fixed amount per unit of the imported product. For example, €2 per imported shoe.
  • Combined tariff: This is a combination of an ad valorem tariff and a specific tariff.

The importer pays the import tariff at customs when the goods enter the country. These costs are then often passed on to the consumer in the price of the product they buy.

docs.title: What is the consequence for the citizens?
docs.text:
The introduction of an import tariff can have several consequences for the citizens of a country:

  • Higher prices: The most direct consequence is that the price of imported goods increases. This can lead to a general increase in prices (inflation), meaning citizens have to pay more for certain products. If there are no or few domestic alternatives, this can significantly impact household budgets.
  • Protection of domestic industry: One of the main reasons for introducing import tariffs is to protect domestic industries from competition from cheaper foreign products. By increasing the price of imported products, domestic products become relatively more attractive, which can lead to increased demand for these products and the preservation or creation of jobs within the country.
  • Less choice: If import tariffs discourage the import of certain goods, this can lead to a smaller supply of products for consumers. Citizens may have less choice and access to specific products that are not produced domestically.
  • Possible retaliatory measures: If one country imposes import tariffs, other countries may retaliate by also imposing tariffs on goods exported from the first country. This can lead to a trade war, where the prices of both import and export products rise, which is detrimental to both consumers and businesses.
  • Increased government revenue: Import tariffs generate revenue for the government. This revenue can be used to fund public services or to reduce other taxes.
  • Stimulation of domestic innovation: By reducing competition from foreign products, domestic companies may be encouraged to innovate and produce more efficiently to better compete, even without the protection of tariffs. However, the opposite can also happen, where protected industries become less inclined to innovate because the pressure from competition decreases.
  • Effects on different income groups: The impact of import tariffs can vary across different income groups. If tariffs are levied on essential goods, this can have a greater impact on lower-income households, who spend a larger portion of their budget on these goods.

In short, import tariffs are a complex tool with both potential benefits (such as protecting domestic industry and government revenue) and drawbacks (such as higher prices and less choice for consumers). The ultimate impact on citizens depends on the specific goods on which the tariffs are levied, the level of the tariffs, and the reaction of other countries.

docs.title: Software Architecture, The Hard Parts - Neal Ford
The Architect's Dilemma: A World of Awful Tradeoffs
docs.text: In his insightful talk, "Software Architecture: The Hard Parts," Neal Ford delves into the core challenges that make the role of a software architect so demanding. The central theme is that there are no easy answers or perfect solutions in architecture; every decision is a complex tradeoff. This talk aims to illuminate these difficult areas and provide frameworks for navigating them more effectively.

docs.title: The Core Challenge: Finding the Right Granularity
docs.text:
At the heart of many architectural puzzles lies the concept of granularity. Getting the size and scope of your components, services, and even teams right is crucial for a healthy, scalable system. Ford illustrates this principle through various lenses:

  • Event-Driven Architectures: How big should an event be? How much data should a service own? The wrong granularity can lead to chatty, co-dependent services or bloated, monolithic ones.
  • Components and Teams: The way you structure your teams often reflects (or dictates) the structure of your software (Conway's Law). Aligning team boundaries with component boundaries is a critical, yet difficult, task.
  • Architectural Quantum: This term refers to an independently deployable component with high functional cohesion. Identifying and building these "quanta" is key to achieving true microservices architecture, but it's a significant challenge.

docs.title: The Myth of Effortless Reuse
docs.text: One of the most tempting promises in software development is reuse. While it sounds simple, Ford explains why achieving effective reuse across an application, a department, or an entire enterprise is one of architecture's "hard parts." What works for a single team often fails to scale because context, dependencies, and communication overhead are vastly different at the enterprise level. The dream of a universal component library often clashes with the reality of diverse business needs and technical constraints.

docs.title: Making Better, Harder Decisions
docs.text: Since architecture is defined by difficult decisions, architects need robust tools for tradeoff analysis. Ford advocates for structured thinking to move beyond gut feelings. He introduces tools like MECE (Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive) lists, a technique to ensure that when you're evaluating options, your criteria are comprehensive and don't overlap. This allows for a more rigorous and defensible decision-making process, ensuring all facets of a problem are considered.

docs.title: Decoupling: The Path to Proper Granularity
docs.text: To achieve the right level of granularity, decoupling is essential. The goal is to design services that are truly independent, allowing them to be developed, deployed, and scaled without creating a domino effect across the system. This talk explores strategies for effective decoupling, which is the foundational work required to make modern, distributed architectures successful.

docs.title: Conclusion: Making the Hard Parts Softer
docs.text:
"Software Architecture: The Hard Parts" doesn't offer magical solutions. Instead, it provides a clear-eyed view of the real-world challenges architects face. By understanding the common root causes of architectural difficulty—like the quest for proper granularity and the complexities of reuse—and by applying structured techniques for tradeoff analysis, we can make the "hard parts" of architecture a little bit softer.

docs.title: Is SaaS Dead?, Here's a Senior Engineer's Perspective
docs.text: "SaaS is dead" became a talking point after Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella used the phrase on the BG2 podcast in December 2024: if AI agents can take over the interface and the work, what is left of a subscription application? In his video, senior engineer Arjan from the ArjanCodes channel argues the opposite for a large part of the market — that the value of many SaaS products sits in work that has nothing to do with the code. This post summarises his argument and adds the figures and documents it leans on.

docs.title: More Than Just Code: The Real Moat of SaaS
docs.text: Arjan's position is that the debate over AI replacing SaaS usually ignores the operational and regulatory work these platforms absorb. An agent can reproduce the functionality of a simple application; it cannot reproduce years of accumulated compliance obligations, integrations and partnerships. The "moat", on his reading, is the messy invisible part.

docs.title: 1. Accounting and Financial SaaS
docs.text: An accounting system looks like a series of calculations, but it is a stack of moving obligations: tax codes per country, state and municipality, security requirements for financial data, and connections to banks and payment rails. That is maintenance, not a one-off problem. Stripe's own product catalogue illustrates the point: Stripe Tax exists solely to "automate sales tax, VAT, and GST compliance on all your transactions" — a product whose reason to exist is that tax rules keep changing.

docs.title: 2. Web Hosting and Infrastructure SaaS
docs.text: Spinning up a server is easy; running one reliably is not. Squarespace, the video's sponsor, documents DoS/DDoS mitigation, a fully-managed cloud platform serving billions of monthly views and 99.9 percent uptime. (An earlier version of this post repeated a 99.99 percent figure; Squarespace's own support documentation states that "no platform can guarantee 100% uptime" and that its public commitment is 99.9 percent.) Content delivery, traffic spikes and attack mitigation are operational work that does not disappear when the code can be generated.

docs.title: 3. Payment Providers
docs.text:
Payment providers such as Stripe and Adyen sell trust and regulation rather than transaction processing. The basis for that is PCI DSS, maintained by the PCI Security Standards Council to "encourage and enhance payment card account data security" — and mandatory in practice for anyone handling card data. PCI DSS applies to every entity that stores, processes or transmits cardholder data, including merchants, processors, acquirers, issuers and service providers, and Adyen's own compliance guide notes that although the standard is not law, "the card schemes" mandate it globally with significant penalties for non-compliance. The certification itself is graded: Stripe states it is certified to PCI Service Provider Level 1, "the most stringent level of certification available in the payments industry".

Two details of that burden are easy to underestimate. First, the standard keeps moving: PCI DSS v3.2.1 was retired on 31 March 2024, and of the 64 new requirements in v4.0, 51 were future-dated and only became mandatory on 31 March 2025. Second, fraud work is measured in money, not features: Stripe says it prevents more than 500 million dollars in payment fraud for its merchants every month.

docs.title: 4. Music and Media Services
docs.text: Streaming is a licensing business with a hosting front. Spotify's own royalties guide describes how money moves through labels, distributors, publishers and collective management organisations — PROs and mechanical agencies — before reaching artists and songwriters, split by territory and by performance versus mechanical rights. The scale of what is being administered: Spotify says it has paid out nearly 70 billion dollars to artists, songwriters and rights holders to date, including 10 billion dollars in 2024, spread across a long tail — 12,500 artists generated more than 100,000 dollars on the platform that year. No AI agent reproduces those contracts.

docs.title: What Does the Future Hold for SaaS?
docs.text:
Arjan's conclusion is that SaaS is not dying but evolving: AI gets integrated into existing platforms, micro-SaaS becomes cheaper to build for small teams, and the regulated, integration-heavy layer remains hard to displace with code alone.

The market data available so far does not show a collapse:

  • Gartner's forecast, reported by CIO Dive and TechRadar, put SaaS spending at 250.8 billion dollars in 2024 rising to 299.1 billion in 2025, within total cloud spending of 723 billion.
  • Synergy Research measured the 2024 cloud infrastructure market at 330 billion dollars, 60 billion more than 2023, with generative AI driving about half of that growth.
  • IDC attributes the "SaaS is dead" line to Nadella's podcast appearance, and its own verdict is that SaaS "is being disrupted, not by decline but by evolution"; it predicts that seat-based pricing will be obsolete by 2028, with 70 percent of vendors repricing around consumption or outcomes.

docs.title: Military spending and the future of Europe, #2006 Lex Hoogduin, Paul Buitink, Kees de Kort
docs.text: In a recent discussion on De Nieuwe Wereld TV, hosted by Ad Verbrugge, economists Lex Hoogduin, Paul Buitink and Kees de Kort addressed some of the most pressing questions of the moment. The focus was on increased military spending, the state of Europe's economy, the future of the euro and the contours of a new financial and economic world order.

docs.title: Never Waste a Good Crisis: The New NATO Target
docs.text: The conversation opens with a critical note on the recent decision to raise military spending to the NATO target of 2% of GDP. The consensus at the table is that, although a stronger defence may be necessary, the current approach smacks of opportunism. The speakers question whether the extra billions will be spent efficiently. There is scepticism about the trading mentality of the arms industry, and concern that business mainly casts hungry glances at the subsidy pots without this actually strengthening defence capability. The debate revolves around the question: are we buying security, or filling the industry's coffers?

docs.title: The European Mindset: Between Complacency and Urgency
docs.text: An important theme that follows from this is whether Europe has the right mindset to face the current geopolitical and economic challenges. The picture is sketched of a continent that for years lived in a comfortable, almost complacent position under the American security umbrella. Now that the world order is shifting, the sense of urgency does not seem to have sunk in everywhere to the same degree. Is Europe willing to make the sacrifices that strategic autonomy requires, or does it remain trapped in internal divisions and bureaucracy?

docs.title: Inflation, Eurobonds and the Role of the Central Bank
docs.text: The economic heart of the discussion is the problem of inflation and the role of the European Central Bank (ECB). The speakers are critical of the policy of recent years. In their view, the low interest rates and the buying up of government debt fuelled inflation and contributed to today's problems. The introduction of eurobonds, that is joint European debt, is seen as a further step towards a transfer union, in which healthy northern economies help finance the debts of the southern countries. This raises fundamental questions about the future and the sustainability of the eurozone.

docs.title: The Euro: Blessing or Stranglehold?
docs.text: This inevitably leads to the question of whether leaving the euro should be an option. Although this subject is often treated as taboo, it is discussed openly at the table. What would the economic consequences of such a step be for a country like the Netherlands? Is it possible to leave the currency union in a controlled way, or would it lead to unmanageable chaos? Opinions are divided, but the conclusion is that the debate about the fundamental design flaws of the euro must continue.

docs.title: Towards a New World Order
docs.text:
Zooming out to the global playing field, the economists discuss the rise of a new financial and economic order. The dominance of the dollar and of the Western financial system is being challenged by emerging powers such as China and the BRICS countries. This shift has major consequences for Europe's position. The question is how Europe should position itself in this new balance of power. Does it remain a loyal ally of the United States, does it seek closer ties with other blocs, or does it try to chart its own independent course?

The discussion, closed with questions from the audience, makes clear that Europe stands at a crossroads. The choices now being made in the field of defence, economics and monetary union will determine the future of the continent for decades.

docs.title: Minimum Viable Architecture, Randy Shoup, YOW! 2022
docs.text:
In the world of software engineering, there's a tempting desire to build the perfect, infinitely scalable architecture from day one. However, as veteran architect Randy Shoup explains in his talk at YOW! 2022, this is often a path to failure. The key takeaway is that architecture is not a static blueprint; it's an evolutionary journey that must align with the changing needs of the business. There is no one-size-fits-all solution.

This post summarizes Shoup's concept of "Minimum Viable Architecture," exploring how your system's design should adapt as your product moves from a simple idea to a globally scaled platform.

docs.title: The Journey of Giants: eBay and Amazon
docs.text:
Shoup begins by looking at the architectural history of giants like eBay and Amazon.

  • eBay (1999): Started as a massive C++ monolith connected to a single, gigantic Oracle database. It was incredibly successful but became a bottleneck, leading to a multi-year re-architecture effort towards a more distributed system.
  • Amazon (2001): Similarly, Amazon began with a monolithic application server connected to a large database. By 2001, this "brittle" architecture was hindering their ability to innovate. This led to the famous mandate from Jeff Bezos to move towards independent, service-oriented teams with clear APIs—the birth of their microservices architecture.

The lesson from these stories is clear: the architecture that gets you started is rarely the one that will sustain you at scale.

docs.title: Phase 1: The "Prototype" - In Search of an Idea
docs.text:
When you're just starting, the primary goal isn't to build a scalable system; it's to validate an idea and find a product-market fit.

  • Goal: Maximize learning and iteration speed.
  • Constraints: Limited time, money, and people.
  • Minimum Viable Architecture: A simple monolith. This could be a single application (e.g., a Rails or Django app) connected to a single database.

At this stage, the biggest risk is building something nobody wants. The architecture should be optimized for rapid development and pivoting, not for handling millions of users. A monolith is perfect for this, as it's simple to build, deploy, and change quickly.

docs.title: Phase 2: The "Just Enough" Architecture - Building the Business
docs.text:
Once you've found product-market fit, the focus shifts to building a sustainable business.

  • Goal: Add features, acquire customers, and build a repeatable business model.
  • Minimum Viable Architecture: A Modular Monolith.

The monolithic structure is still the right choice for most companies at this stage, as it keeps the team focused and efficient. However, it's crucial to enforce modularity within the monolith. Think of it as creating "namespaces" or "packages" with well-defined boundaries inside the single codebase. This discipline prevents the monolith from becoming an unmanageable "big ball of mud" and paves the way for future evolution.

During this phase, establishing engineering excellence is key. Practices like Continuous Delivery and the use of Feature Flags are vital. They decouple deployment from release, allowing you to ship code continuously while controlling what users see, which is essential for both testing and incremental rollouts.

docs.title: When Is It Time to Re-architect?
docs.text: Moving away from the monolith is a significant, expensive, and risky decision. Shoup emphasizes that you should only do it when you have no other choice. The primary driver is usually organizational scaling. When your engineering team grows so large that the monolith becomes a bottleneck to productivity—with teams constantly stepping on each other's toes—it's time to consider a change.

docs.title: Phase 3: The "Scalable" Architecture - From Monolith to Microservices
docs.text:
When the pain of the monolith outweighs the pain of re-architecting, you enter the scaling phase.

  • Goal: Scale the organization and the system.
  • Minimum Viable Architecture: Microservices.

The move to microservices allows you to scale your teams independently. Each team can own a service (or a set of services), allowing them to develop, deploy, and scale their part of the system without being blocked by others.

Shoup stresses the importance of an incremental migration. A "big bang" rewrite is almost always a mistake. Instead, follow a proven pattern: 1. Don't rewrite, refactor: Gradually carve out services from the existing monolith. 2. Identify seams: Use the modules you defined in the "Just Enough" phase as natural boundaries for your new microservices. 3. Extract services one by one: Pick a component, build it as a separate service, and strangle the old monolithic implementation by redirecting calls to the new service. 4. Use an event-driven approach: Asynchronous events are excellent for decoupling services and ensuring resilience.

docs.title: Phase 4: The "Stable" or "Optimizing" Architecture
docs.text: Once the migration is largely complete, the architecture enters a more stable phase. The goal shifts to optimizing for cost, performance, and resilience. This might involve fine-tuning services, exploring different data stores, or investing in more sophisticated infrastructure. The key is that the architecture is now flexible enough to allow for continuous, targeted improvements.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The concept of a Minimum Viable Architecture teaches us that software architecture is a living thing. By matching your architecture to the current phase of your business, you can avoid premature optimization and focus your resources on what truly matters at each stage. Start simple, maintain modularity, and only embrace the complexity of distributed systems when the pain of your current success forces you to.

docs.title: C4 models as code, Simon Brown, NDC Oslo 2023
The Agony of Outdated Architecture Diagrams
docs.text:
We've all been there. You're trying to understand a complex system, and you finally hunt down the architecture diagrams, only to be hit with a soul-crushing realization: they haven't been updated since the project's kickoff. The diagrams show a pristine monolith, but you know for a fact that the reality is a sprawling jungle of microservices, serverless functions, and cryptic third-party integrations. The documentation lies, and the "source of truth" is now just a source of confusion.

This is the problem that Simon Brown, the creator of the C4 model, tackles in his brilliant talk from NDC Oslo 2023. While "Diagrams as Code" tools like PlantUML and Mermaid have been a huge step forward, they often have a fundamental flaw when used at scale.

docs.title: The Flaw of "Diagrams as Code"
docs.text:
Tools like PlantUML allow us to write text that generates a diagram. This is great! We can now version control our diagrams, diff them, and embed them in our documentation pipelines.

However, they are diagram-centric. Each .plantuml file typically describes a single diagram. If you want to show the same microservice in a high-level system context view and a more detailed container view, you end up defining that microservice in two separate files.

Now, multiply that by a dozen services and five different views for each. What happens when a service is renamed? You have to hunt down and update every single file where it's mentioned. This manual effort leads to inconsistencies, and before you know it, you're right back where you started: with outdated, untrustworthy diagrams.

docs.title: A Better Way: Models as Code
docs.text:
Simon Brown presents a powerful paradigm shift: move from "Diagrams as Code" to "Models as Code".

Instead of writing files that describe diagrams, what if we wrote a single file that describes the model of our software architecture? We define all the building blocks—the people, software systems, containers (applications, databases, etc.), and components—and the relationships between them, all in one place.

This is precisely what the open-source Structurizr DSL allows you to do.

docs.title: How Structurizr Works
docs.text:
With the Structurizr DSL, you create a central definition of your architectural elements. It looks something like this (in pseudocode):

// Define the elements in your model
user = person "Customer" "A user of our system"
ecommerceSystem = softwareSystem "E-commerce Platform" {
  webapp = container "Web Application" "Handles user requests"
  database = container "Database" "Stores product and order info"
}

// Define the relationships
user -> webapp "Uses"
webapp -> database "Reads from and writes to"

Once you have this central model, you can create as many different views (diagrams) as you need, all from the same source of truth. You simply tell Structurizr what you want to see in a particular diagram.

// Define a System Context diagram
systemContext ecommerceSystem {
  include * // a wildcard to include all top-level elements
  autoLayout
}

// Define a Container diagram
container ecommerceSystem {
  include * // show all containers within the e-commerce system
  autoLayout
}

If you rename the "Web Application," you only have to change it in one place in the model. Every single diagram that includes it is automatically updated. Boom. Consistency restored.

docs.title: The Key Benefits
docs.text:
1. Single Source of Truth: Your model is the truth. Your diagrams are just views of that truth.
  2. Consistency Guaranteed: No more drifting between different diagrams.
  3. Separation of Concerns: The model (the content) is separate from the view (the presentation). You can even render your model using different tools like PlantUML, Mermaid, or Structurizr's own tooling.
  4. Full Automation: Because it's all text, you can integrate it into your CI/CD pipeline to ensure your architecture documentation is never out of date.

By treating your architecture as a model, you transform your documentation from a static, decaying artifact into a living, breathing part of your system that evolves right alongside your code.

docs.title: Huizenmarkt op slot: 'iemand moet de prijs betalen' | Jona van Loenen
docs.text: In aflevering #2010 van De Nieuwe Wereld praat econoom en columnist Jona van Loenen met Jelle van Baardewijk over de Nederlandse woningmarkt. Zijn stelling is dat het tekort aan huizen de prijzen niet opdrijft, maar de hoeveelheid geld die een koper kan lenen of meeneemt. Die bewering staat naast het beleidsmotto van het afgelopen decennium, bouwen, bouwen, bouwen, en ze gaat gepaard met voorstellen die de kosten naar woningbezitters verschuiven.

docs.title: De stelling: financieringsruimte, niet het tekort
docs.text:
Het betoog van Van Loenen begint met een vergelijking die in de cijfers te controleren valt. In 2021 daalde het geraamde woningtekort van 331.000 naar 279.000 woningen, terwijl de huizenprijzen dat jaar met 15,2 procent stegen, de grootste stijging in 21 jaar. Als het tekort de prijzen opdreef, zo redeneert hij, dan zouden die twee cijfers niet de tegengestelde kant op moeten bewegen. Het mechanisme dat hij beschrijft: het aanbod van woningen beweegt nauwelijks mee met de vraag, dus concurreren kopers vooral op hoeveel ze kunnen betalen, en dat bedrag volgt uit de rente, de inkomens en de leennormen.

Hij beroept zich op onderzoek van De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) en herhaalt die verwijzing in een column in de Volkskrant (29 augustus 2024) en in zijn boek over erfenissen en vermogen.

docs.title: Wat die DNB-analyse werkelijk zegt
docs.text:
De analyse waar Van Loenen naar verwijst is Financieringsruimte en huizenprijzen (Eijsink & Van Dijk, DNB, 2023). De conclusie: de financieringsruimte is de belangrijkste drijver van de huizenprijzen, en andere factoren, zoals nieuw aanbod, zijn in hun model niet significant. Een eenmalige stijging van de financieringsruimte met 3,5 procent leidt in dat model na ongeveer 20 kwartalen tot 3,9 procent hogere huizenprijzen, een elasticiteit dicht bij 1. De analyse merkt ook op dat de prijzen tussen juni 2013 en juni 2022 nagenoeg verdubbelden, vooral gedreven door de rente (de gemiddelde hypotheekrente daalde van 3,7 naar ongeveer 1,7 procent) en door de inkomens (meer dan 30 procent hoger).

Hetzelfde document voegt een nuance toe die de korte versie van het betoog weglaat. Bouwen beweegt de prijzen in het model van DNB niet, maar de analyse stelt dat structurele bouw wel bijdraagt aan betere toegankelijkheid, oftewel aan wat een starter zich werkelijk kan permitteren. Het beleidsadvies van DNB wijst de andere kant op dan het stimuleren van de vraag: ruimere leennormen voor starters werken een-op-een door in hogere prijzen, en daarom pleit de bank ervoor die niet te verruimen.

docs.title: De cijfers waar het gesprek op stuit
docs.text:
• Prijzen. Bestaande koopwoningen piekten in juli 2022, werden ongeveer een jaar goedkoper (in mei 2023 lagen ze 5,8 procent onder het niveau van een jaar eerder) en stijgen sinds juni 2023 weer. In 2025 waren bestaande woningen 8,6 procent duurder dan in 2024, en in december 2025 lagen de prijzen 13,9 procent boven de piek van juli 2022, met een gemiddelde verkoopprijs van bijna 486.000 euro in het vierde kwartaal (CBS/Kadaster).
  • Tekort. Het ministerie van Volkshuisvesting (BZK) raamt het statistisch woningtekort voor 2026 op 384.000 woningen, ofwel 4,6 procent van de voorraad, na 4,9 procent in 2024 en 4,8 procent in 2025. Het ministerie beschouwt een tekort van rond 2 procent als een aanvaardbare spanning; om die te halen zijn ongeveer 213.000 extra woningen nodig.
  • Het patroon. De prijzen daalden toen de rente steeg, in 2022-2023, en herstelden terwijl het tekort groot bleef. Juist die combinatie maakt het debat lastig te beslechten met één enkele reeks: de twee bewegen niet een-op-een samen.

docs.title: De voorstellen die hij op tafel legt
docs.text:
Van Loenen pleit niet voor een bouwstop. Hij betoogt dat bouwen alleen de huizen niet goedkoper maakt, en dat de waarde die in bestaande woningen is opgebouwd belast of afgewaardeerd moet worden. In het gesprek en in zijn columns noemt hij een hogere overdrachtsbelasting, een belasting op de overwaarde die verkopers meenemen naar hun volgende aankoop, strengere grenzen aan de leencapaciteit en een forse verhoging van de erfbelasting. Hij zet die maatregelen neer als een correctie op wat hij een onverdiende overdracht van vermogen tussen generaties noemt, niet als begrotingsmaatregelen.

Elk van die maatregelen herverdeelt, en het gesprek werkt niet uit wie de kosten draagt. DNB berekende in dezelfde analyse uit 2023 dat een prijsdaling van 20 procent ongeveer 8 procent van de woningen met een hypotheek onder water zou zetten, ruwweg 300.000 huishoudens, vooral recente kopers, met een hypotheek die groter is dan de waarde van het huis. Strengere leennormen verkleinen eerst wat starters kunnen lenen. Een belasting op woningvermogen komt terecht bij de groep die het huis al heeft betaald, en de opbrengst hangt af van tarieven die nog altijd een politieke keuze zijn.

docs.title: Wat het gesprek niet beslecht
docs.text:
Dit is een gesprek, geen studie: één gast, geen tegenspreker aan tafel, en de voorstellen zijn de zijne. Wat de beschikbare cijfers openlaten, is of het beperken van de financieringsruimte op zichzelf de prijzen omlaag brengt of vooral de wachtrij verschuift (minder huishoudens die kunnen kopen, langere wachtlijsten in de huursector), en hoe een bewuste prijscorrectie uitpakt voor de ongeveer vier miljoen huishoudens met een hypotheek. Het gesprek blijft ook weg van de timing: de Nederlandse prijzen stijgen al acht kwartalen op rij terwijl het tekort langzaam afnam, het omgekeerde patroon van wat beide kanten van het debat bij één enkele oorzaak zouden voorspellen.

docs.title: Why Tech Platforms Intentionally Work Worse, The Enshittification Phenomenon
docs.text:
Ever wondered why your favorite tech platforms, once sleek and user-friendly, now feel bogged down with an endless stream of ads and questionable content? You're not alone! For centuries, this barrier seemed insurmountable, dictating the maximum velocity a ship could achieve. However, human ingenuity, driven by the thrill of competition and the desire for faster transport, led to groundbreaking innovations. The video traces the exciting rise of racing yachts and the intense evolution of the America's Cup, a crucible of design and engineering where every rule and limitation was rigorously tested and often circumvented.

The video takes us into the chaotic realm of cavitation – the formation of vapor bubbles in a liquid due to pressure changes, which can lead to significant drag and even damage. This seemingly insurmountable obstacle pushed engineers to think outside the box, leading to revolutionary designs. One of the most astounding examples is the "Sailrocket," a futuristic vessel that defies traditional boat shapes to achieve astonishing speeds, essentially flying on water and leaving the cavitation barrier in its wake. This incredible feat highlights the power of unconstrained thinking in engineering.

Ultimately, this exploration isn't just about sailing fast; it's a testament to human curiosity and the drive to innovate. It showcases how challenging assumptions and pushing against perceived limits can lead to breathtaking advancements, redefining what's possible on the open water. docs.title: An AI Research Assistant Promises Citation-Backed Drafts. A Study Counted Fabricated References.
docs.text:
Of 636 citations in 84 AI-generated literature reviews, 55 percent of the GPT-3.5 ones pointed at papers that do not exist. That is the number to hold next to a sales pitch.

In a webinar on the AnswerThis channel, co-founder and CMO Ryan McCarroll shows an AI research assistant that searches the literature, drafts citation-backed text and summarises papers. The pitch is speed: literature work that took weeks, in minutes. The claim comes from the vendor. This post sets it against the studies and the rules that followed.

docs.title: What the company sells
docs.text:
AnswerThis describes itself as "an all-in-one AI research assistant that supports your entire workflow, from finding research gaps and collecting papers to summarizing, analyzing, and drafting citation-backed content for your research paper, dissertation, or thesis".

The demo is about finding gaps in the literature, mapping citations between papers, and a first draft of a literature review with references attached. The company says that work which used to take months now takes minutes. Its Y Combinator profile describes the platform as used by over 200,000 researchers.

The company's own pages do not agree on how many people use it. The homepage speaks of "1 Million+ researchers" and a "300M+ paper" database, while the pricing FAQ says 250M+ papers. A million on one page, two hundred thousand on another.

It is a paid product. The pricing page lists a free tier, a Pro tier at 35 dollars per seat per month and institutional licences. Annual-billing tiers run from 0 to 100 dollars.

A citation-map feature, a benchmark against Google Scholar or PubMed, and the claim of "more than 20 citations in minutes" appear only in the vendor's own pages. They are vendor claims, not measured results.

All of it comes from the company.

docs.title: What the studies counted
docs.text:
A fake reference looks just like a real one.

A peer-reviewed study in Scientific Reports (Walters & Wilder, 2023) examined 636 bibliographic citations in 84 AI-generated reviews. It found that 55 percent of the GPT-3.5 citations and 18 percent of the GPT-4 citations were fabricated. None of them existed. Of the real ones, 43 percent (GPT-3.5) and 24 percent (GPT-4) contained substantive errors.

A second study in the Journal of Medical Internet Research (Chelli et al., 2024) asked the models to reproduce systematic reviews. It measured hallucinated references at 39.6 percent for GPT-3.5, 28.6 percent for GPT-4 and 91.4 percent for Bard. LLMs, the authors concluded, should not be used "as the primary or exclusive tool for conducting systematic reviews".

AnswerThis sells the citation. In both studies, the citation is the part that failed.

docs.title: Rules instead of bans
docs.text:
Publishers wrote rules. ICMJE states that chatbots and other AI tools cannot be listed as authors. They cannot answer for accuracy, integrity and originality. Authors must review and edit AI output, which the guidance notes "can be incorrect, incomplete, or biased". COPE says the same: AI tools "cannot meet the requirements for authorship". Over 200,000 researchers use a tool that cannot be listed as an author.

The universities are blunter. Erasmus University Rotterdam tells staff and students not to use GenAI to look up or check facts. A plausible answer is not a reliable one. Amsterdam's policy states that GenAI output is not a reliable academic source.

Ghent University's framework lists invented references among the known limits. Antwerp's guidelines note that AI texts often lack proper sourcing or carry invented citations. Harvard's FAS guidance requires any use of AI to be acknowledged and cited. The student answers for the result.

The rules differ. They agree that the tool writes and the person signs.

docs.title: What to do with a tool like this
docs.text:
Treat these references as leads, not sources. Open every citation before it goes into your bibliography. Confirm the DOI, the journal and the year. Keep that check inside the workflow. A bibliography is where a fake becomes a plagiarism case.

Check your institution's rules before you start. They differ on acknowledgment, permitted use and the responsibility clause. Ask the vendor for the audit trail. A tool that shows where a citation came from is a different product from one that only writes the sentence.

docs.title: The Line: a 170-km City Announced, a 2.4-km First Phase Planned
docs.text:
In 2022 Neom presented a city 170 kilometres long, 200 metres wide and 500 metres high. It was called The Line. Nine million people were supposed to live inside it, without cars or roads, on renewable power, at an official cost of around $500 billion.

The first phase now on the internal plans is 1.5 miles. At least $50 billion has already been spent, and the desert it stands in is marked by piling and deep trenches.

This post sets an architectural analysis of that design against the reporting on what has been built and paid for since. The analysis is Daniel Titchener's, from August 2025.

docs.title: The design that was announced
docs.text:
The published plans describe two parallel towers forming one continuous wall. The horizontal transport runs inside the structure rather than on the surface, so the city has no outside street at all.

Neom's own framing was that this layout would replace the outward growth of conventional cities with a structure the length of a country. Residents would reach services within a short walk. The drawings also include a marina, a stadium above it and a building suspended upside down from an arch. Reporting has questioned all three.

Those are the drawings. Titchener's question is a different one: can anyone live inside a wall?

docs.title: Titchener's argument
docs.text:
Titchener works through three themes, and all three are his reading of the design rather than findings about the construction site. The first is sprawl, inverted. Where a conventional city expands outward, The Line constrains everything along one axis. Internal high-speed transit then has to carry all movement. The enclosure leaves little room for the incremental expansion and change that cities normally absorb.

The second is liveability. Stand on an inner face and you lose daylight and ventilation. The varied street-level surroundings that an ordinary city provides are gone. Vertical farming and integrated services are offered as compensation. They are plans, not demonstrated practice.

The third is perfection. The structure is engineered from a fixed specification in one direction, which leaves little space for the adaptations a city acquires over decades. Titchener argues that the rigidity is a design risk in its own right.

Those are architectural objections. The reporting that follows is about money and schedule.

docs.title: The Financial Times
docs.text:
The Financial Times traced The Line through interviews with more than twenty people who worked on it. They were architects, engineers and former senior executives. The piece ran on 6 November 2025. It found that at least $50 billion has been spent. The desert is marked by piling and deep trenches, and the first phase has been scaled back sharply.

The same reporting gives the internal budget estimates. They moved from $1.6 trillion in late 2021 to around $4.5 trillion in the spring of 2022. Both figures describe the same project. The official estimate was around $500 billion. Only the smallest one was public.

docs.title: The Wall Street Journal
docs.text:
The Wall Street Journal reported that the first phase is now planned at roughly 1.5 miles of structure by 2030. That is 2.4 kilometres, and the approximately 10 miles previously envisioned is no longer the plan. Internal expectations for the first phase run below 200,000 residents. The announcement said nine million. A draft board presentation put the capital needed to build out Neom to its end state by 2080 at $8.8 trillion.

Neither the residents figure nor the capital figure appears in a published plan.

docs.title: CNBC
docs.text:
CNBC reported in July 2025 that the Public Investment Fund had engaged consulting firms for a strategic review of The Line's feasibility. The fund finances Neom. Neom confirmed the review and described such checks as common practice on long-term projects.

The fund holds the kingdom's own money. A shorter line therefore comes out of a national budget rather than out of a company's balance sheet. The fund that pays for the project is now asking whether the project works.

docs.title: What Neom says
docs.text:
Neom told the Financial Times that The Line remains "a strategic priority". Neom said the project would ultimately "provide a new blueprint for humanity by changing the way people live", and called it a "multi-generational development of unprecedented scale and complexity". The company says attention has moved to "the complex engineering and detailed design work associated with the first phase".

Faisal Al Ibrahim, the Saudi minister of economy and planning, was asked about the shortened first phase in a CNBC interview. His reply was that "there is no change in scale — it is a long-term project that is modular in design". He added that the kingdom does not want to overheat its economy. Neom's deputy chief executive Rayan Fayez said the project's budget "evolves every day".

The internal plan has the first phase at 1.5 miles. None of those three answers contains a figure.

docs.title: The step not taken
docs.text:
No cancellation of The Line has been announced. Neom has not published a revised master plan, budget or timeline, so the figures above come from internal documents and from people involved rather than from official releases.

The step that would make the project hard to reverse is awarding the contracts for the construction above ground. According to the Financial Times, that step had not been taken. A shortened first phase could still be a staging post, or it could be the practical end of the 170-kilometre plan.

The completed groundwork is the other open question. Nobody has said what happens to it if the vertical building does not follow.

docs.title: The Real Reason AI Is Going Back to the Terminal
docs.text: In the space of six months in 2025, four major AI vendors shipped coding agents that run in the terminal: Anthropic's Claude Code (24 February), OpenAI's Codex CLI (16 April), Google's Gemini CLI (25 June) and Cursor's CLI (7 August, in beta). The tool that looked like a step backwards — a prompt in a shell instead of a chat window — is where these companies put their agentic coding effort. This post looks at what they actually shipped, what the terminal is used for in the design, and which parts of the "return to the terminal" story are documented rather than assumed.

docs.title: What shipped, and when
docs.text:
• Claude Code (Anthropic, 24 February 2025). Announced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet as "a command line tool for agentic coding", initially in limited research preview: developers "delegate substantial engineering tasks to Claude directly from their terminal".
  • Codex CLI (OpenAI, 16 April 2025). Introduced with o3 and o4-mini as "a lightweight coding agent you can run from your terminal"; the repository describes it as "lightweight coding agent that runs in your terminal" under Apache-2.0.
  • Gemini CLI (Google, 25 June 2025). Open source under Apache 2.0, and — in Google's own words — "brings Gemini directly into developers' terminals".
  • Cursor CLI (Cursor, 7 August 2025). Announced in beta as "our new terminal-based agentic coding agent".

Four launches in one year is a pattern; the word "back" needs care. None of the announcements describes the move as a strategy of returning to something. What they describe is a capability: an agent that can act on a machine, which is easier to give a shell than a browser window. The interpretation that this is a deliberate retreat from graphical interfaces is an inference from the products, not a stated plan.

docs.title: Why the terminal works for an agent: the loop
docs.text:
The technical reason the shell is a good fit is what those products do in it. Simon Willison's working definition of an agent is "something that runs tools in a loop to achieve a goal", and the useful part for coding is that the agent can verify its own work: these agents "can now directly exercise the code they are writing, correct errors, dig through existing implementation details, and even run experiments to find effective code solutions to problems".

Anthropic describes the same design decision from the inside: "We found that by giving Claude access to the user's computer (via the terminal), it had what it needed to write code like programmers do." The loop itself is documented as: Claude evaluates the prompt, calls tools to take action, receives the results, and repeats until the task is complete. A shell is where those tools already live — file system, build, test runner, version control — which is why the interface converges there rather than in a chat pane.

docs.title: Why it spreads beyond the terminal
docs.text:
The other half of the shift is that the terminal agent is often the engine behind other interfaces:

  • Anthropic states that "the agent harness that powers Claude Code (the Claude Code SDK) can power many other types of agents, too", and renamed that SDK the Claude Agent SDK; its documentation says the SDK gives developers "the same tools, agent loop, and context management that power Claude Code, programmable in Python and TypeScript".
  • JetBrains' Claude Agent inside its IDEs is described as "advanced AI coding assistance built on Anthropic's Agent SDK, which powers Claude Code".
  • Claude Code itself now runs on several surfaces: "the terminal, IDE extensions, a desktop app, and the web".

So a fair version of the claim is: the terminal agent and its SDK became a layer that graphical clients build on, in the cases that have been published. The stronger version — that this is the backbone of almost every AI interface — is not supported by the sources reviewed here.

docs.title: What this means if you write software
docs.text:
• The interface is a detail; the loop is the product. An agent that can run your tests and read the failure is a different tool from one that only writes text about them, and the terminal is where the difference shows up first.
  • Permissions become the design question. Handing an agent a shell hands it your machine; the loop is only useful because it can act.
  • Expect CLI-first, then GUI. The pattern in the four examples above is a terminal tool first, then plugins, desktop and web clients on the same harness — useful to know when you are choosing what to integrate with.

docs.title: From "Coder" to "Conductor": How AI is Rewriting Software Development
docs.text:
Imagine sitting at your desk, but instead of staring at a blinking cursor and manually typing out lines of code, you feel more like an orchestra conductor. You aren't writing the notes anymore; you are guiding an entire crew of AI agents.

That is precisely the shift software creator Peter Steinberger highlights in his work. Rather than casual "vibe coding," he calls his approach agentic engineering. He barely writes code by hand anymore; instead, he designs systems, establishes the core architecture, and lets AI agents handle the boring plumbing work.

docs.title: From Pull Requests to Prompt Requests
docs.text: The most radical part of his workflow? He often doesn't even read the code he ships. While traditional software engineering relies heavily on meticulous code reviews and pull requests, Steinberger views contributions now as prompt requests. The real value lies in the underlying intent and how effectively you prompt the AI, not the raw text generated. As long as a robust feedback loop—where the system automatically runs tests and catches errors—is in place, the output becomes reliable.

docs.title: The "Black Eye Club"
docs.text: Working this way is intensely addictive. Steinberger talks about the "Black Eye Club"—developers staying up until the early morning hours because prompting AI feels like playing a slot machine. The thrill of entering a prompt and getting an ingenious solution back is hard to put down. However, it is also mentally exhausting, requiring you to constantly context-switch while managing five to ten active agents in parallel.

docs.title: A Word of Caution
docs.text:
Before you throw away your IDE, Steinberger offers a reality check. There is a steep learning curve to mastering the "language of the machine," and many experienced developers burn out early because they expect instant magic without learning how to steer an agent properly. Furthermore, building a side project is entirely different from an enterprise environment; large companies need a massive cultural and structural refactor before AI can truly scale efficiently.

Ultimately, tomorrow's developer looks less like a manual bricklayer and more like an architect—someone who commands an army of digital builders with a single prompt.

Source: The creator of OpenClaw: "I ship code I don't read"

docs.title: The Memory Price Surge: Why RAM and Storage Got So Expensive
docs.text: If you've shopped for RAM or a new SSD lately, you've probably felt a sting. The same 32 GB DDR5 kit that cost a comfortable amount a year ago now costs noticeably more, and that 2 TB NVMe drive you had your eye on keeps creeping up in price. This isn't your imagination or a supply chain blip — 2026 is witnessing one of the most dramatic memory price rallies in the industry's history, and it all traces back to one thing: AI.

docs.title: The AI Memory Boom
docs.text:
Artificial intelligence is devouring memory at an unprecedented scale. Every AI accelerator — from NVIDIA's GPUs to custom inference chips — relies on High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), the ultra-fast stacked memory that feeds models their data. Demand for HBM has exploded so much that the three memory giants (Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron) are reallocating their production capacity toward the high-margin HBM stacks used in data centers, squeezing the supply of conventional DRAM and NAND flash used in your laptop, phone, and server.

In short: the wafers that used to become your DDR5 modules and SSD chips are increasingly being turned into AI memory instead.

docs.title: The Numbers Are Staggering
docs.text:
The price action over the past year has been historic. TrendForce expected average DRAM prices to rise between 50% and 55% in Q1 2026 alone, and contract prices for conventional DRAM were projected to climb another 58–63% in Q2 2026 after that historic rally. J.P. Morgan Global Research estimates DRAM prices will have risen more than 400% from the start of 2024 to the end of 2026.

NAND flash is following the same trajectory — in Q2 2026, NAND contract prices were expected to jump 70–75% quarter-over-quarter, actually outpacing DRAM for the first time in this cycle. Analysts have even coined a term for it: "memflation." One estimate puts the year-over-year increase at roughly 125% for DRAM and a stunning 234% for NAND flash, meaning a storage array quoted at the end of 2025 costs more than double to provision by the end of 2026.

docs.title: Who Feels the Pain
docs.text:
The effects ripple through the entire industry. PC and smartphone makers are facing sharply higher component costs, which IDC warns will reshape specs and pricing across the 2026 device market — think less RAM in budget phones, or higher price tags for the same specs. Data center operators are seeing their build-out costs balloon, which eventually trickles down to the price of cloud services. Even the automotive and IoT sectors, which rely on mature-node memory, are feeling the squeeze as manufacturers deprioritize those lines.

And then there's the consumer. Enthusiasts building a new PC are facing RAM and storage costs that can rival the CPU, and the secondhand market has turned into a frenzy of its own.

docs.title: Signs of Cooling
docs.text:
There is some relief on the horizon. By Q3 2026, the surge has begun to slow as consumers hit their affordability limits: TrendForce projects conventional DRAM contract prices to rise a "modest" 13–18% quarter-over-quarter, with NAND flash up 10–15% — substantial gains, but a marked slowdown compared to earlier in the year.

Still, this is a slowdown, not a reversal. The structural driver — AI capex and HBM's share of fab capacity — remains firmly in place. As long as data center spending keeps growing, conventional memory will keep competing for wafer space.

docs.title: What Should You Do?
docs.text: If you've been postponing a RAM or storage upgrade, there's a reasonable case for buying sooner rather than later. Prices may keep climbing through the rest of 2026, even if at a gentler pace. Keep an eye on contract-price reports, shop around, and consider locking in components before your next build — memory has quietly become one of the most expensive parts of a modern system.

docs.title: It's Happening: Europe Is Building an Impossible Fusion Reactor
docs.text:
Proxima Fusion has €411 million to build the shape the fusion world walked away from. The Munich startup, spun out of the Max Planck Institute, counts Google and energy giant RWE among its backers. Its reactor is a stellarator: a twisted "donut" so absurdly complicated it was long believed impossible to build.

For fifty years the tokamak has dominated fusion research. The classic donut-shaped reactor is the design that gets the money. Proxima is betting everything on the other one, and on a plan to build the first stellarator power plant in history. The money is already committed. The cage is not built, and that gap decides whether fusion ever reaches a grid. Everyone who pays an electricity bill is downstream of that question.

docs.title: A Cage That Leaks
docs.text:
Fusion means slamming atomic nuclei together until they merge. That takes 100–150 million degrees Celsius, and no material can touch it. So the plasma has to hang suspended in a magnetic cage. There is nothing to catch it. The magnets are the only thing between that heat and the wall of the vessel.

The simplest cage is a donut-shaped torus, and it leaks. The field is stronger on the inside of the ring. Ions and electrons drift apart until the plasma pushes itself into the walls. Nothing in the machine survives contact with the plasma. The field is the wall, and it is only as good as its twist.

The fix is a helical twist in the field lines. The stellarator is the shape that provides that twist on its own. Every machine in this story is an argument about how to get it.

docs.title: The Design the World Walked Away From
docs.text:
The tokamak gets its twist by running a current through the plasma itself. That made it easy to build, and in 1968 the Soviet T-3 convinced the world to abandon stellarators almost overnight.

What the world took on instead comes with a timer. A transformer only works while the current is changing, so every tokamak runs in pulses. ITER, the largest fusion project on Earth, aims for burns of about 400 seconds before it needs a timeout. Fine for science, fatal for a power plant. Anyone waiting on fusion electricity is waiting on a machine that runs for hours, not for 400-second bursts.

Not everyone left. A small group at the Max Planck Institute kept working on the stellarator, and their Wendelstein 7-X finally proved the physics of the absurd shape. In 2023 it held a 40-million-degree plasma for eight full minutes. But W7-X can never produce more energy than it consumes. It is a physics experiment, and the gap to a power station is the whole problem.

The tokamak won the money. The stellarator won the physics.

docs.title: Proxima's Cheat Code: Stronger Magnets
docs.text:
Proxima's bet is that fusion power scales with the fourth power of the magnetic field. Double the field, and the power goes up 16 times.

W7-X's niobium-titanium magnets quit past 12 tesla, so Proxima uses REBCO, a high-temperature superconducting tape pioneered by MIT and Commonwealth Fusion Systems. Its design runs at around 9 tesla on-axis, against W7-X's 2–3: roughly 81 times the potential output.

The roadmap: a full-scale test coil in 2027, a demonstration reactor called Alpha targeting net energy gain in the early 2030s, and 50 power plants by 2050. Industrial heat and the neutrons for medical isotopes are the returns along the way. The grid is the prize.

That is what the €411 million is buying. If the tape holds, the stellarator comes back. If it does not, the shape the world walked away from stays gone.
