docs.title: Tipping in America: How a $2.13 Wage Floor Became Everyone's Checkout Prompt
docs.text:
Tipping in the United States no longer waits for the end of a sit-down meal. It turns up on tablet checkouts at coffee counters, in ride-hailing apps, on delivery screens and, in some places, at self-checkout kiosks. In a Pew Research Center survey from November 2023, 72% of American adults said tipping is expected in more places than it was five years earlier.

Underneath that spread sits a structure most diners never see. The federal wage floor for tipped workers has been $2.13 an hour for more than three decades. State laws cut across it, and the federal rules around it were rewritten twice in two years.

The custom is old. The arithmetic behind the prompt is not.

docs.title: A custom that arrived late
docs.text:
Tipping began in medieval Europe and only took hold in the United States after the Civil War. Millions of formerly enslaved people entered the labour market at that moment. In an episode of NPR's history podcast Throughline from April 2021, the journalist Nina Martyris describes what happened next. Restaurant owners opening in Chicago and New York were "looking for cheap labor," and hired the new workers as waiters and cooks. "They didn't pay them because this tipping system had come in, and they had to make their wage through tips".

The practice was contested from the start. Many Americans of that era called tipping "racist, aristocratic, antilabor, demeaning". A handful of states passed anti-tipping laws, which the programme notes proved almost impossible to enforce.

In 1916 William Rufus Scott published The Itching Palm, the polemic Martyris calls the most famous one against the practice. Its verdict has worn well: "tipping is the price of pride. It is what one American is willing to pay to induce another American to acknowledge inferiority".

The habit outlasted the laws written against it.

docs.title: The $2.13 floor
docs.text:
American tipped work rests on the tip credit. Congress created it in 1966 by amending section 3(m) of the Fair Labor Standards Act (Public Law 89-601). An employer may count part of a worker's tips toward the minimum wage, capped at 50% of it. The same law defined a tipped employee as someone who customarily and regularly receives more than $20 a month in tips.

According to the Congressional Research Service, those amounts stayed a percentage of the minimum wage, between 40% and 60%. The 1996 amendments replaced the percentage with a fixed figure of $2.13 an hour. The figure has not moved since.

The Department of Labor's fact sheet for tipped employees describes how that works. The employer pays at least $2.13 an hour directly. The rest of the $7.25 federal minimum may come from the customer's tips, up to a credit of $5.12. If tips plus the direct wage fall short of $7.25 in a workweek, the employer must top up the difference. Where state law differs, the employer follows the standard most protective to employees.

Several states do differ. Alaska, California, Minnesota, Montana, Nevada, Oregon, Washington and Guam require the full state minimum wage to be paid before tips. Those floors run from Minnesota's $11.41 to Washington's $17.13. The District of Columbia still allows a credit: an $18.40 minimum wage, $8.10 in cash and a $10.30 credit. One Fair Wage, which campaigns against the subminimum wage, counts 43 states that permit "some version of the subminimum tipped wage".

An employer may count a customer's generosity as wages.

docs.title: Two years of rewriting
docs.text:
The regulatory detail has been unstable. In 2021 the Department of Labor restricted the tip credit to work that is part of the tipped occupation. Directly supporting work no longer counted once it passed 20% of the workweek or 30 continuous minutes.

On 29 October 2024 the Fifth Circuit vacated that revision. The court held that it "fails under the Administrative Procedure Act twice over," contrary to the text of the statute. The panel added that the rule was arbitrary and capricious. The underlying "80/20" guidance dates from a 1988 handbook. The department issued a technical final rule on 17 December 2024 restoring the older text.

Federal tax treatment changed as well. An IRS tax tip from January 2026 notes that employees and the self-employed may deduct qualified tips, up to $25,000 a year. The deduction phases out above $150,000 in modified adjusted gross income, and above $300,000 for joint filers. It took effect for the 2025 tax year. Its effect on how tips are reported, or on how much customers leave, has not been measured.

Cities have moved on their own terms. The Chicago City Council voted on 20 May 2026 to delay its One Fair Wage phase-out by two years, freezing the subminimum at $12.62 against a city minimum of $16.60.

Two years of rewriting left the floor where it was.

docs.title: What the screens ask for
docs.text:
Prompting for a tip is now largely a software default. Pew notes that "the adoption of point-of-sale tablets, apps and digital kiosks has made it easier for businesses to provide customers with tip prompts and suggestions". The vendor documentation shows who chose the numbers.

For a transaction of $10 or more, Square's options are "No Tip, 15%, 20% or 25%," while merchants can configure up to three percentages. The API defaults to 15, 20 and 25. The setting that shows the tip screen at the counter, before the card is put away, is on by default.

Toast lets merchants edit three percentages, but online ordering displays four suggested amounts by default. If a check already carries a mandatory gratuity, the system "will automatically take this into account and suggest an additional 3%, 5%, and 7% tip," amounts it calls fixed.

Clover allows at most four suggestions. Its developer example configures 18%, 20%, 25% and 30%, labelled "Acceptable", "Good", "Great" and "Excellent".

None of those numbers came from the customer.

docs.title: What the customers say
docs.text:
Customers keep answering the same questions, and the answers have drifted. Pew found in 2023 that 92% of sit-down diners say they always or often tip there. 57% would leave 15% or less for an average meal. Habitual tipping drops sharply elsewhere: 25% for coffee, 12% at fast-casual restaurants. More adults oppose tip suggestions (40%) than favour them (24%). Automatic service charges do worse: 72% oppose them regardless of group size, against 10% in favour.

Bankrate's June 2025 survey found 63% of Americans holding at least one negative view of tipping, up from 59% a year earlier. Two answers came in at 41% each: that businesses should pay better instead of relying on tips, and that tipping culture has got out of control. The drift shows in habits as well. 70% always tip sit-down servers, against 75% in 2021. Among Generation Z that share is 43%. Among Generation X it is 83%.

The people serving the tables report the same confusion. A poll of nearly 50 hospitality professionals in August 2025 found 54% saying the service fees restaurants add, typically 15% to 22%, confuse guests. Only 8% thought those fees help secure fair wages.

Popmenu, a restaurant technology vendor, surveys 1,000 consumers twice a year. It found 65% "fed up" with tipping in September 2025, against 53% in 2023. By March 2026, 78% called the practice ridiculous, and 44% said they were tipping less than the year before. On Popmenu's own platform, the share of pickup orders carrying a digital tip fell from 78% in 2022 to 62% in 2026, a drop of 16 percentage points.

Smaller surveys point the same way. PYMNTS Intelligence found 75% of consumers calling a tip option at self-checkout inappropriate. Oobit found 82% calling a self-checkout tip request unreasonable, and 37% who had stopped visiting a business over aggressive prompts. Upgraded Points found 90% saying tipping has got out of hand.

At the till, the levels have moved less than the mood. Toast's platform data for the third quarter of 2025 put the average tip at 19.2% in full-service restaurants and 15.8% in quick-service. The full-service figure sits just above the seven-year low of 19.1% from the previous quarter. Delaware tipped highest at 21.1%, California lowest at 17.2%.

The gap between what customers say and what the terminals ask keeps widening.

docs.title: Two readings of the same industry
docs.text:
The BLS puts the median hourly wage for waiters and waitresses at $16.94 in May 2025, across about 2.3 million jobs. For the broader group of food and beverage serving and related workers the median is $15.24, against $24.51 for all other occupations.

The National Restaurant Association, which represents the industry, projects sales of $1.55 trillion in 2026 and employment of 15.8 million. It argues that the tip credit means "tipped workers never make less than the prevailing minimum wage". The association also says that "nationally, tipped servers take home a median of $27 an hour, with the highest-paid making more than $41 an hour".

One Fair Wage counters that the federal tipped wage has been $2.13 "since 1991," and that 43 states still allow a subminimum.

Both organisations have a position in the debate. They measure different things: a median across all hours worked including tips, and a statutory floor. Whether the tipped-wage model on balance helps or hurts the people who work under it remains contested by the parties to it.

A median and a statutory floor are not comparable numbers.

docs.title: What the research finds
docs.text:
Academic work is less flattering to the idea that tips track service. A meta-analysis by Michael Lynn and Michael McCall covered 22 published and 14 unpublished studies. The size of the bill turned out to predict the tip better than the quality of the service. In their words, bill size was "the single largest predictor of tip size in restaurant settings," and it accounted for twice as much variability as all other factors combined.

Server attractiveness, friendliness and customer mood came next. Service quality, server effort and cost consciousness were "reliable, but weak".

Lynn's later framework lists five motives behind tipping. They run from helping servers and rewarding service to gaining social esteem and fulfilling felt obligations. Economists, he notes, have treated the practice as irrational or mysterious. Tips to American restaurant workers alone are estimated at about $44 billion a year.

A second line of research asks who gets tipped. Lynn and colleagues reported in 2008 that customers of both races tipped Black service providers less than White ones. They raised the possibility of unlawful adverse impact. Brewster and Nowak (2019) estimated that the average Black customer leaves about 3.30 percentage points less than a White customer. That finding is not settled. Brewster, Gourlay and Nowak (2022) ran three survey experiments. They found no evidence that consumers tip Black servers less than comparable White servers, all else being equal.

The published answers point in opposite directions.

docs.title: Guilty Until Proven Sick: A Patient-Advocacy Reel and the Data on Diagnostic Delay
docs.text:
She was a former marathon runner, "super active", and then she started blacking out while sitting at her desk. She went from doctor to doctor. What she heard was that it was "probably anxiety, depression, maybe it's your cycle". Her answer was that she knew what anxiety felt like, and that "this feels different".

A year of misdiagnosis and mismedication followed. She ended up needing a pacemaker. By the time a woman she had never met spoke with her, she had just turned 30 and had undergone five heart surgeries, for what her doctor said could have been prevented if it had been caught sooner.

We know this because Amanda Rose Berk repeated it in a 101-second Instagram reel on 15 September 2026. The phrase she credits to that caller is the one doing the work: guilty until proven sick. That is what it feels like when your symptoms have to be proven before anyone takes them seriously.

There is no name, no hospital, no diagnosis, no record in the post. The case cannot be checked from it. It is one person's account of a conversation.

The reel is also patient advocacy with a product attached. Its caption calls the problem "a huge part of why we're building LIORA" and points to a waitlist. So here is what the reel claims, next to what the published record says about diagnostic delay.

docs.title: What the record shows
docs.text:
Diagnostic error is measured, and its size is that of a disease. An analysis by the Johns Hopkins Armstrong Institute Center for Diagnostic Excellence, with the Risk Management Foundation of the Harvard Medical Institutions, appeared in BMJ Quality & Safety in July 2023. It estimated that about 795,000 Americans die or are permanently disabled by diagnostic error each year: 371,000 deaths and 424,000 permanent disabilities, across hospital and clinic settings.

Heart attacks are the documented case of that gap. Researchers looked at 564,412 patients, over nine years, who were ultimately diagnosed with a heart attack. Around a third had received an initial diagnosis that differed from the final one. Women who ended up with the more severe STEMI type had a 59% greater chance of an initial misdiagnosis than men. For NSTEMI the figure was 41%.

The British Heart Foundation, which published the summary in August 2016, describes the same finding: women are roughly 50% more likely than men to get an incorrect initial diagnosis after a heart attack. Put plainly, a woman's first answer is wrong more often than a man's, for the same event.

That is not a niche condition. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention states that heart disease is the leading cause of death for women in the United States, and that over 60 million women, 44%, live with some form of it. So if you are a woman, the misdiagnosis figures above are not an edge case. They are the odds you would meet if you arrived at a hospital with a heart attack.

The mechanism the reel describes, symptoms filed under mental health, shows up in patient-facing material too. The Canadian Heart & Stroke Foundation writes that "one study showed that women who mention stress along with physical symptoms of cardiac disease are much more likely to be diagnosed with anxiety than men reporting exactly the same thing." The article does not name the study, so the research behind that sentence is not identified there.

docs.title: What the patient has to do about it
docs.text:
The reel also lists the labour the patient takes on. Track every symptom. Do the research. Find the right doctors. Collect referrals. Retell the story. And try not to seem "too informed, too anxious", or like someone who Googled too much.

That list is the quiet companion of the statistics. A system that gets the first answer wrong in a third of cases does not take the problem back from the patient. It hands the problem to the person in the waiting room, and asks her to be credible while she does it.

docs.title: What the reel cannot establish
docs.text:
The reel offers no numbers and cites no research. The national estimates above are aggregates across all patients and all conditions, and they say nothing about one person's experience. Whether the caller's outcome was in fact preventable, and whether her symptoms were dismissed because she is a woman, is not something a published source here can confirm.

The record supports something narrower, and still uncomfortable. Diagnostic error harms hundreds of thousands of Americans a year. In one large UK dataset, women were more likely than men to be told something else first. And the story that carries the phrase cannot be checked at all.

One more thing worth noting. The reel is promotional, and a health claim travels with a waitlist link.

docs.title: Geen enkele dierentuin verloor ooit zijn vergunning: wat Nederland nu wil veranderen
docs.text:
"Tot op heden is het echter niet voorgekomen dat een dierentuinvergunning gedeeltelijk of geheel is ingetrokken door de minister." Die zin staat in De toekomst is er zoo, de zienswijze van de Raad voor Dieraangelegenheden, het adviesorgaan van de overheid zelf. Op de peildatum had Nederland 59 instellingen met een dierentuinvergunning, en geen enkele daarvan is er ooit een kwijtgeraakt.

Op 12 oktober 2026 maakte het ministerie van Landbouw, Visserij, Voedselzekerheid en Natuur bekend dat het stelsel op de schop gaat. De visiebrief erachter is op 9 oktober ondertekend door staatssecretaris Silvio Erkens en wil een stelsel herschrijven dat sinds 2003 staat. Twee lezingen doen de ronde. De ene zegt dat periodieke toetsing het stelsel eindelijk tanden geeft. De andere zegt dat het rechtsonzekerheid oplevert en een kostenbasis die bij grote parken past.

Ik ben de stukken nagegaan om te zien welke lezing standhoudt. Allebei, en dat is het interessante deel.

docs.title: Hoe het stelsel nu werkt
docs.text:
De Nederlandse vergunning voert de Europese dierentuinrichtlijn (1999/22/EG) uit, via hoofdstuk 4.1 van het Besluit houders van dieren. Artikel 4.2 lid 1 verbiedt het exploiteren van een dierentuin zonder vergunning van de minister. Artikel 4.4 eist een inspectie voordat die vergunning wordt verleend. Artikel 4.10 verplicht de houder bij te dragen aan het behoud van soorten. Artikel 4.13 geeft een tuin een redelijke termijn van ten hoogste twee jaar om een situatie te herstellen voordat de vergunning kan worden ingetrokken.

RVO verleent de vergunningen en vraagt advies aan de Visitatiecommissie Dierentuinen. De NVWA doet de inspecties. Een gewone aanvraag duurt acht weken, met de mogelijkheid tot zestien.

Wat er nu ligt is een stelselwijziging, geen nieuw stelsel. Eerst het vergunningensysteem, mede om de regeldruk te verlagen, daarna de inhoudelijke thema's. De brief noemt er elf: het vergunningensysteem, regeldruk, dierenwelzijn, de omgang met surplusdieren, publieksinteracties, educatie, dierpresentaties, conservatie, wetenschappelijk onderzoek, veiligheid, en curatieve en preventieve veterinaire zorg. Het instrument is een wijziging van hoofdstuk 4.1 van het Besluit houders van dieren. De brief noemt het geheel "een ambitieuze en omvangrijke stelselwijziging". Een ontwerpbesluit of wetsvoorstel is er nog niet.

docs.title: Een vergunning voor onbepaalde tijd
docs.text:
De scherpste kritiek op het stelsel komt van de eigen adviesraad van de overheid, niet van dierenrechtenorganisaties. In de zienswijze van 26 maart 2025 stelt de Raad voor Dieraangelegenheden vast dat vergunningen voor onbepaalde tijd worden afgegeven: "Dat betekent dat dierentuinen die niet veranderen hun vergunning behouden." Alleen wijzigingen worden opnieuw beoordeeld. En: "Het gevolg is dat dierentuinen via het vergunningstelsel nauwelijks bijgestuurd worden naar nieuwe inzichten ten aanzien van dierenwelzijn en de doelen van dierentuinen."

De raad vindt dat onwenselijk en beveelt aan het stelsel aan te passen, "bijvoorbeeld met een vaste periodieke herbeoordeling of door het overstappen naar een systeem met vergunningen voor bepaalde tijd". Zijn eigen waarneming zet hij er in één regel bij. De vergunning die nooit is ingetrokken, is de vergunning die nooit is hertoetst.

De brief van het ministerie herhaalt die diagnose in steviger bewoordingen. Een tuin die niets doet, houdt zijn verouderde vergunning. Alleen vernieuwende tuinen worden opnieuw getoetst, en "daarmee wordt de regeldruk vooral gevoeld door de dierentuinen die vooruit willen". Het doel is dat vooroplopers niet worden geremd en achterblijvers worden aangespoord, mogelijk met zelfregulering door de vooroplopers.

docs.title: Wat de raad niet meet
docs.text:
Dat periodieke toetsing het welzijn verhoogt, is in deze stukken een aanname en geen bevinding. De raad redeneert over prikkels. Wat hij wel vastlegt, is een ontwerpprobleem in de huidige regels: "sommige open normen in het wettelijk kader, bijvoorbeeld ten aanzien van het veterinair protocol, leiden tot ongewenste welzijnsrisico's."

Hetzelfde geldt voor de sturing op inspanning. Bij een aanvraag moet een beleidsprotocol over conservatie en educatie worden ingediend, en "deze protocollen zijn inspanningsgericht. Het huidige wettelijk kader is niet gericht op de output van dierentuinen op de geformuleerde doelstellingen." Daardoor loopt de werkelijke impact van tuinen op die doelen ver uiteen.

Dat is een belangrijk verschil. De inhoud van de norm kan zwaarder wegen dan hoe vaak er wordt gecontroleerd.

De raad signaleert ook welzijnsrisico's bij dieren achter de schermen, waar het publiek nooit komt. Hun verblijven zijn vaak niet diersoort-specifiek en ze worden bij de vergunningverlening niet beoordeeld. De NVWA werkt vooral meldingsgericht, "maar meldingen zijn minder waarschijnlijk in situaties waar dieren afgeschermd zijn van het publiek". De dieren die je nooit ziet, zijn dus ook de dieren waarover het minst wordt gemeld.

De handhavingscijfers zijn dan ook niet dierentuinspecifiek. Het jaarbeeld 2025 van de NVWA meldt 4.418 welzijnsinspecties bij 3.136 unieke bedrijven, tegen 4.095 inspecties in 2024, zonder uitsplitsing naar dierentuinen. De Dierenbescherming schreef in maart 2025 dat niet alle soorten het even goed hebben in dierentuinen, dat sommige soorten zichtbaar verbetering nodig hebben en andere misschien helemaal niet in een dierentuin passen, en dat een algemeen oordeel daardoor lastig is.

docs.title: Het Dolfinarium als proefveld
docs.text:
Het meest uitgewerkte handhavingsdossier is het Dolfinarium, en het laat zien hoe moeilijk de huidige regels te hanteren zijn. De staatssecretaris legde op 28 maart 2025 een last onder dwangsom op wegens overtreding van het Besluit houders van dieren en de vergunningvoorschriften. De voorzieningenrechter schorste die in mei 2025, omdat het bewijs niet overtuigend genoeg was. Zowel de staatssecretaris als zijn deskundige had videofragmenten beoordeeld zonder het volledige educatieve programma van de tuin mee te wegen.

In september 2025 werd een tweede besluit terzijde geschoven als onvoldoende zorgvuldig voorbereid en onvoldoende gemotiveerd, in strijd met de artikelen 3:2 en 7:12 van de Algemene wet bestuursrecht. Het Dolfinarium had daarbij gewezen op rechtszekerheid en het vertrouwensbeginsel.

Op 6 oktober 2026 deed het College van Beroep voor het bedrijfsleven drie uitspraken in zaken van het Dolfinarium, en ze wijzen verschillende kanten op.

In zaak 25/727 en zaak 25/865 verklaarde het College het beroep gegrond en vernietigde het het bestreden besluit. Het herriep het dwangsombesluit, omdat daaraan "geen deugdelijke en controleerbare vaststelling van relevante feiten en omstandigheden ten grondslag ligt". Ook kwam het besluit niet met de zorgvuldigheid van artikel 3:2 van de Algemene wet bestuursrecht tot stand. Aan de vraag of de interacties in strijd waren met de vergunning kwam het College daardoor niet meer toe.

In zaak 25/206 ging het de andere kant op. Daar verklaarde het College het beroep ongegrond, omdat de vergunning niet toestond dat dolfijnen op commando naar bezoekers toe kwamen zodat die ze konden aanraken. De staatssecretaris was dus bevoegd een dwangsom op te leggen.

Dat is het meest concrete materiaal in het dossier over rechtszekerheid, en het snijdt twee kanten op. De hoogste bestuursrechter bevestigt dat handhaving deugdelijke en controleerbare feiten vraagt, en dat slordige voorbereiding een besluit vernietigt. Dat beschermt vergunninghouders. Het is ook een waarschuwing dat een open norm niet meer waard is dan het bewijs erachter. In één zaak uit de reeks was de norm duidelijk genoeg voor een dwangsom; in twee andere was het bewijs dat niet.

RVO erkent de wrijving zelf. Op de pagina over de proef met vooroverleg voor verblijven, gecontroleerd op 1 oktober 2026, staat dat een vooroverleg "u meer duidelijkheid kan geven over de soms complexe aanvraagprocedure voor een wijziging van uw vergunning". Sinds de eerste openstelling in januari hebben twee dierentuinen zo'n vooroverleg gehad. Er is nog plaats voor zeven andere, en bij de selectie let RVO op een afspiegeling van de sector, inclusief tuinen die niet bij een van de twee landelijke verenigingen zijn aangesloten.

docs.title: Wie betaalt, en wie zit er aan tafel
docs.text:
Geen enkel stuk in dit dossier meet wie de kosten draagt van strengere, periodiek getoetste vergunningen. Wat de raad wel vastlegt, is hoe ongelijk de sector is gebouwd.

Van de 59 instellingen met een vergunning op peildatum 1 maart 2025 zitten er dertien in de NVD, die zegt dat zijn leden samen ongeveer tien miljoen bezoeken per jaar trekken. Veertien zitten in Dier en Park, de vereniging van kleinere regionale dierenparken. Ongeveer de helft van alle vergunde tuinen is bij geen van beide aangesloten. De eigen RVO-lijst van 4 augustus 2026 telt 60 instellingen.

De verschillen in omvang zijn groot. Een stuk of vijf tuinen trekken meer dan een miljoen bezoekers per jaar, terwijl sommige kleinere rond de 25.000 bezoekers ontvangen. Enkele tuinen beslaan meer dan 150 hectare; een vlindertuin of aquarium past in een paar honderd vierkante meter.

Verschillende tuinen horen bij grotere concerns. Libéma bezit Safaripark Beekse Bergen, Eindhoven Zoo, Zoo Parc Overloon en AquaZoo Leeuwarden. Het Spaanse Aspro Parks, met 68 recreatielocaties in tien landen, bezit het Dolfinarium en Deltapark Neeltje Jans. In kleine tuinen is de eigenaar vaak tegelijk directeur, manager en dierverzorger.

Het ministerie weet dat. De brief merkt op dat de twee verenigingen ongeveer de helft van de sector vertegenwoordigen en veruit de meeste bezoekers trekken, en zegt dan: "De dierentuinen waarop aanpassing van de regelgeving mogelijk de grootste impact zal hebben, zijn echter niet verenigd."

docs.title: Geen ontwerp, geen termijn, geen bedrag
docs.text:
Er is geen ontwerpwijziging. Er is geen gepubliceerde termijn voor vergunningen, geen definitie van de "meetbare educatieve bijdrage" die de brief vraagt, en geen kostenraming van wat een geldigheidsduur of periodieke herbeoordeling voor een kleine instelling betekent.

De welzijnswinst is ontworpen, niet gemeten. Het beste handhavingsmateriaal, de Dolfinariumzaken, is een reeks vernietigingen op procedure in plaats van beslissingen over de inhoud. Wel noemt de staatssecretaris een concrete vervolgstap: "Met name in het verlagen van de regeldruk voor dierentuinen en de omgang met surplusdieren verwacht ik de komende maanden concrete stappen te zetten."

Beide lezingen overleven het dossier dus. Je kunt het lezen als een stelsel dat nooit werd hertoetst en dat nu wel wordt. Of als een set open normen waarvan de kosten en de duidelijkheid zaak per zaak in de rechtszaal worden vastgesteld. De vooroplopers helpen de regels mee schrijven, en de minst georganiseerde helft van de sector kijkt vanaf de zijlijn toe. Die helft houdt de dieren waar het publiek niet komt.

docs.title: What Big Tech, Pharma and Food Companies Pay Where They Sell
docs.text:
Amazon's European retail entity booked 51.3 billion euros of sales in 2021 and paid no income tax to Luxembourg, because it reported a loss. That is all in the filings, and it is legal.

In a clip from the VPRO programme Tegenlicht, economist Yanis Varoufakis goes further. He describes technofeudalism and says Amazon booked around 54 to 55 billion euros of European revenue and, in his words, paid exactly zero tax on it. Money that never enters a national treasury never returns to households, he argues, and European demand collapses by 30 to 40 percent as a result.

The first claim can be checked against the documents. The second cannot. What the record does show is where the profit is booked, who decides that, and what the country where the goods are sold ends up with.

docs.title: Apple: a rate of 0.005 percent
docs.text:
Start with the number that is hardest to believe. In 2011 Apple's subsidiary Apple Sales International recorded 22 billion dollars of profit. Under the tax rulings it operated on, roughly 50 million euros of that was considered taxable in Ireland, which left 15.95 billion euros untaxed. Apple paid less than 10 million euros in Irish corporate tax that year, an effective rate of about 0.05 percent on its total annual profit. By 2014 that rate had fallen to 0.005 percent, according to the European Commission.

The Commission's conclusion in August 2016 went further than one company's rate. In its words, "the tax treatment in Ireland enabled Apple to avoid taxation on almost all profits generated by sales of Apple products in the entire EU Single Market". Ireland had granted undue tax benefits of up to 13 billion euros, and had to recover them.

The case then took eight years. The General Court annulled the decision in July 2020 because the Commission had not proven a selective advantage to the required legal standard. On 10 September 2024 the Court of Justice set that judgment aside and confirmed the 2016 decision. Commissioner Vestager called it "a big win for European citizens and for tax justice".

The money followed, slowly. Apple's public country-by-country report for fiscal 2025 lists 213.6 billion dollars of revenue in Ireland, 34.6 billion dollars of pre-tax profit and 5,575 employees. The 17.08 billion dollars paid to Ireland that year sits far above the 4.78 billion dollars of tax accrued. Apple explains the difference: escrowed funds were released to Ireland under the state aid decision, with the corresponding expense already taken in fiscal 2024.

docs.title: Amazon: the entity that reported a loss
docs.text:
The numbers in the clip sit closest to Amazon EU Sarl. That entity books e-commerce for the UK, Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Poland, Sweden and the Netherlands in Luxembourg. It recorded 44 billion euros of sales in 2020 and 51.3 billion in 2021. In both years it reported a loss, 1.2 billion and 1.16 billion euros, and therefore paid no income tax to Luxembourg. Bloomberg reported from the filings that it also received one billion euros in tax credits in 2021.

Brussels tried the same route here and lost it. In 2017 the Commission ordered Luxembourg to recover around 250 million euros of undue benefits. On 14 December 2023 the Court of Justice annulled that decision: the Commission had not established that the ruling was incompatible state aid.

Amazon does not accept the broader reading. "Across Europe, we pay corporate tax amounting to hundreds of millions of euros," the company said in response to the Luxembourg reporting. Both statements can be true at once. The entity in the filings owed nothing, and the group says its European entities together pay hundreds of millions. The tax is real, and it lands somewhere other than where the sales happen. Under the rules that apply, the country where the customer clicks to buy has no claim on it.

docs.title: Pharma: 75 percent of the income is offshore
docs.text:
The American evidence is blunt: a Senate committee had the Joint Committee on Taxation compute industry rates from SEC filings. Pharmaceutical companies went from an average worldwide effective rate of 19.6 percent in 2014 to 2016 down to 11.6 percent in 2019 and 2020. Their US domestic rate fell from 27.0 to 15.7 percent over the same period.

Where the income is reported is the point. By those same figures, 75 percent of all Big Pharma income is reported offshore for tax purposes. For non-manufacturing companies the foreign share of taxable income is 22 percent; for non-pharma manufacturing it is 45 percent.

In 2021 the effective rate of every one of the seven largest US pharmaceutical corporations was below 15 percent, well under the 21 percent statutory rate. Johnson & Johnson: 8.3 percent. Pfizer: 7.6 percent. Merck: 11 percent.

Pfizer's own accounting is the clearest case. In 2019 it sold 20 billion dollars of drugs to US customers and reported zero dollars of taxable US profit, telling the IRS that 100 percent of its income was earned offshore. Its effective rate stayed between 5.3 percent and 9.6 percent over those years. Senator Ron Wyden, who commissioned the investigation, called it a scheme that "could be the largest tax-dodging scheme in the history of Big Pharma". Pfizer disputes that characterisation.

AbbVie shows the mechanics. The company holds the intellectual property rights to Humira in a Bermuda subsidiary and manufactures in Puerto Rico. Because US tax law treats Puerto Rico as foreign, that income is taxed at the GILTI rate of 10.5 percent rather than 21 percent. A Senate report in 2022 found that AbbVie booked 99 percent of its taxable income offshore while generating 75 percent of its sales from US patients.

The IRS is now pursuing Amgen over 24 billion dollars of income it says was shifted to Puerto Rico subsidiaries, seeking 10.7 billion dollars in back taxes and penalties. In 2021 Amgen generated 70 percent of its sales in the United States and reported 28 percent of its pretax income there.

One caveat applies here. The Senate material is Democratic staff work that names specific companies. The data underneath comes from the companies' own 10-K filings; the interpretation and the framing are the committee's.

docs.title: Food: the cases that went the other way
docs.text:
Food and drink is where the pattern breaks. Two cases did go against the companies here, and both were unwound on appeal.

Luxembourg recovered 23.1 million euros from Fiat, and the Netherlands recovered 25.7 million euros from Starbucks, after the 2015 decisions. The General Court annulled the Starbucks decision in 2019 because the Commission could not prove that an advantage existed. In 2022 the Court of Justice annulled the Fiat decision because the Commission had applied the arm's length principle and the reference framework incorrectly. The same methodological problem ended the Engie case in 2023.

The published rates for the sector sit at or above what the law asks. Coca-Cola reported an effective rate of 17.4 percent for 2023, AB InBev 25.2 percent, Nestlé 24.6 percent for 2025, Unilever 29 percent.

Those rates do not settle the matter. Coca-Cola has been fighting the IRS for years over transfer pricing, and in November 2020 the US Tax Court predominantly sided with the IRS. Coca-Cola told investors that continuing the disputed methodology would raise its effective rate by about 3.5 percentage points.

The narrowest case of all is McDonald's. In December 2015 the Commission opened an investigation into McDonald's Europe Franchising, which had paid no corporate tax in Luxembourg since 2009 despite profits above 250 million euros in 2013. Three years later it closed the case without a recovery, because the cause was a mismatch between Luxembourg and US tax laws rather than special treatment by Luxembourg.

Then came the sentence that describes the whole field: "Of course, the fact remains that McDonald's did not pay any taxes on these profits, and this is not how it should be from a tax fairness point of view."

docs.title: What the new rules require
docs.text:
Profit shifting is not primarily a matter of fraud. The European Parliament's research service calls transfer pricing the mispricing of resources or intellectual property, so that costs land in high-tax countries and revenues in low-tax ones. On shell entities, the Commission put it plainly: legal entities without minimal substance "continue to pose a risk of being used for improper tax purposes".

Three rules now bite. The Pillar Two directive, adopted in December 2022, collects a top-up tax whenever a multinational group's effective rate in a jurisdiction falls below 15 percent. It applies to groups with at least 750 million euros of revenue, from fiscal years starting on or after 31 December 2023.

The public country-by-country reporting directive requires large multinationals to disclose, per EU member state and per non-cooperative jurisdiction, how much tax they pay and where. It starts with the first financial year beginning on or after 22 June 2024. ATAD caps interest deductions at 30 percent of EBITDA and closes hybrid mismatch arrangements.

The first public reports are arriving, and the EU Tax Observatory has found a pattern: a large group of companies filed reports covering a single member state, Romania, rather than the whole group. PepsiCo's Romanian subsidiaries told the register that they had asked the parent for the global data and that "PepsiCo Inc. did not make this information available to the subsidiaries". The register is filled in by the companies themselves, so the public's view of where the tax goes depends on the parties who choose where it goes.

Estimates differ by method. The OECD puts the annual global cost of base erosion and profit shifting at 100 to 240 billion dollars, equal to 4 to 10 percent of global corporate income tax revenue. It adds one qualification: "although some BEPS schemes are illegal, most are not."

The Commission estimates 35 to 70 billion euros lost each year in the EU, and the Tax Justice Network puts global losses at 492 billion dollars a year. The OECD also expects BEPS activity to fall by roughly half under a minimum tax, with countries collecting around 150 billion dollars more each year.

The counter-move came in June 2025. The US Treasury secured a "side-by-side" arrangement under which American-parented groups are excluded from the two main Pillar Two rules. The carve-out leaves the rules in place and takes a large share of the tax base out of them.

docs.title: Where the clip's numbers drift
docs.text:
The revenue figure in the clip does not match the record. The Luxembourg filings document 44 billion euros of European sales in 2020 and 51.3 billion in 2021. Neither is 54 or 55 billion, and the headline figure for 2021 circulated as dollars rather than euros.

The "zero tax" claim is true for one entity and one tax. Amazon EU Sarl paid no income tax to Luxembourg in 2020 and 2021 because it reported losses. It is not true of the group's European tax bill as a whole, and Amazon says so itself.

The claim that European demand collapses by 30 to 40 percent does not appear in any source I could find, primary or secondary. It is the analytical part of the argument rather than a measurement, and reading it as data would be a mistake.

The two big cases make that last point for me. Apple's ended with a 13 billion euro recovery confirmed at the highest level. Amazon's ended with the Commission's decision annulled. The law asks whether a selective advantage was proven, not whether tax was paid, and those two questions produced opposite answers in two cases that look identical from the outside.

docs.title: The Menopause Cliff: Hormones Shift a Decade Earlier Than the Textbooks Said
docs.text:
The final menstrual period is one of the most consequential days in a woman's endocrine life, and nobody writes it down. That missing date is why the timeline of menopause stayed wrong for a generation. Without it, every lab result is stamped with an age, and two women of 51 can be ten years apart in their transition.

A team at the Weizmann Institute of Science found a way around the missing date. Their paper appeared in Nature Medicine on 12 October 2026, and it changes the shape of the transition. At the final period, 52 of 90 laboratory tests jump. Not bend. Jump, in a step, inside a window of a year or two.

docs.title: The date nobody wrote down
docs.text:
The obstacle is bureaucratic before it is biological. No laboratory database records the day a woman's periods stop, so any curve plotted against age smears out. Two women born in the same year may be a decade apart in their hormone status, and averaging them erases the very moment you want to see.

Uri Alon and his colleagues borrowed a tool from astronomy. If you know how menopause ages are distributed in a population, you can treat that spread as a known distortion. Astronomers sharpen a blurred telescope image the same way. Subtract the smear and every test can be plotted against time to the final period instead of age.

They applied the method to two independent datasets. The first is NHANES, the American health survey that has run from 1999 to 2022. The second is the laboratory archive of Clalit, which insures roughly half of Israel and holds 1.3 million women aged 30 to 70 between 2004 and 2024. Together they hold more than 300 million lab tests. Ninety different tests went in, 57 of them present in both cohorts.

The data was already there. It sat in insurance records for two decades because nobody had asked it a question with a date in it.

docs.title: What jumped
docs.text:
Women showed a statistically significant jump in 52 of the 90 tests, measured against men of the same age spread. The biggest steps sit in bone metabolism, liver enzymes, lipid handling and osmolality, the measure of how the body balances fluid. Ferritin, an iron storage marker, rises by 0.6 standard deviations at the final period. For a curve built from a million people, that is a big step.

Men showed no jump at all. Run through the same algorithm with the same age distribution, their markers slide along a gentle slope. That comparison is what turns a statistical artefact into a physiological claim. An ageing effect would show up in both sexes. This one does not.

The American and Israeli cohorts agree, despite different lab vendors and different populations in two countries.

Some of the change moves in a welcome direction. Iron and haemoglobin improve after the final period, most likely because monthly blood loss stops.

docs.title: The hormones leave first
docs.text:
The reproductive hormones depart long before the cliff edge. According to the Nature press release, anti-Müllerian hormone falls sharply around 15 years before the final period. Follicle-stimulating hormone climbs around 14 years before it, and estradiol drops around 12 years before. For a woman whose last period lands at 50, the hormonal shift starts somewhere around 35 to 38.

That roughly doubles the old estimate. The paper cites the Study of Women's Health Across the Nation, known as SWAN, as the work it is arguing with. SWAN showed that sex hormone changes begin about seven years before menopause, on a few hundred women followed closely. The new reconstruction reaches back twice as far on far more people and far less detail per person.

A woman told to expect seven years of drift may dismiss what begins in her late thirties. That gap between seven and fifteen years is the practical core of the paper.

docs.title: Bone, heart and mood
docs.text:
The American survey also records diagnoses, and those follow the same shape. Osteoporosis prevalence picks up slope at the final period, then outpaces men. Heart attack and stroke accelerate after menopause too. Both match the laboratory signal in bone and lipid markers, which is what you want to see before you believe a finding.

Mood shows a spike and then a partial recovery. Moderate to severe depressive symptoms on the PHQ-9 scale reached 19% in the year after the final period. In the following 24 years the rate was 11%, with a p-value below 10⁻⁴. The denominators matter here: 46 of 236 women in that first year, against 698 of 6,495 later on. It is a real signal from a small group, reported as a transient rise.

Sleep behaves the same way. Difficulty falling asleep climbs after the transition and then settles back toward the male curve. The gap between men and women narrows in several places once the transition is done.

Bone loss and shifting lipids do not announce themselves. They are found, or they are not.

docs.title: Hormone therapy and the women who chose it
docs.text:
Women using menopausal hormone therapy showed markedly smaller jumps, particularly in bone, liver and kidney markers. Read plainly, that is an argument for starting treatment earlier than current practice does. Scientific American's coverage raises exactly that possibility, and adds that more research is needed first.

The paper is more careful than the headline version. Only about 9% of the American women in the dataset used hormones, mostly oral preparations, and they differ from the rest in ways no adjustment fully captures. Access to care, symptom severity and health behaviour all push in the same direction. The authors name healthy-user bias as a limitation themselves.

One detail deserves attention. Hormone therapy appeared to normalise most systems, yet it came with elevated CRP, a marker of inflammation. That fits an older finding about first-pass liver metabolism: oral estrogen raises CRP production, transdermal patches largely do not. Hormone therapy overall is anti-inflammatory, so the delivery route changes the lab picture.

docs.title: The window you may already be in
docs.text:
The practical takeaway concerns timing. If the hormonal phase begins in the mid-thirties and the visible cliff lands around 50, then the decade in which a baseline is most useful is the decade in which almost nobody orders one.

What that baseline looks like is not exotic: a lipid panel, a liver panel, a conversation about bone risk, and a depression screen. All of it is standard, cheap and available. The argument for doing it earlier comes from the shape of the data, not from a new test.

The uncomfortable part is arithmetic. By the time the cliff appears in a blood test, the shift behind it has been running for years, quietly, in a phase nobody had a reason to look at.

Two cautions belong next to that advice. No guideline changed because of this paper, and the authors call for prospective trials before the hormone therapy signal becomes clinical guidance. A population average also says nothing about one woman's timeline, and the spread between women in this data is wide.

Mary Claire Haver, the gynaecologist whose Instagram reel carried the study to a wide audience this week, makes the same point about her own practice. She does not wait for the last period before looking.

docs.title: What the method cannot tell you
docs.text:
This is a reconstruction from cross-sections, not a cohort that followed women through the transition. Instead of watching one person age, the authors pooled thousands of snapshots taken at different distances from the final period and let the algorithm put them in order.

The payoff is scale: 90 tests, two countries, a million women, 25 years. The cost is interpretation. Everything here describes the average path of a population. It cannot tell a 42-year-old what her own estradiol did last year, and it cannot tell a doctor when a specific patient crossed a threshold. The authors list retrospective data, self-reported menopause timing and the limits of deconvolution among their own caveats.

The causal question stays open as well. The link between hormone therapy and smaller jumps is consistent with a protective effect, and equally consistent with healthier women choosing treatment. Randomised trials settled a version of that question for bone two decades ago. They will be needed again for the wider picture.

The authors close by asking for the prospective study that follows individual women through the cliff. Until that exists, the sharpest picture of the transition sits in lab results that were already in an insurance database.

docs.title: Software Isn't Dead, Generic Software Is
docs.text:
For fifteen years Chris Ashby designed apps and advised startups on product. In a 35-minute video on his channel Build Great Products he makes an uncomfortable claim for anyone still shipping a generic dashboard: your product might not make it. Building one is now a weekend job with Claude Code or Codex, and what used to make software defensible, the fact that it was expensive and slow to build, has evaporated.

His conclusion is not that software is finished. It is narrower: software is not dead, generic software is. What follows is his list of eight shapes that still have room, and where that argument is solid and where it is a forecast.

docs.title: Three shifts behind the argument
docs.text:
Ashby puts the change on three shifts. First, building got cheap, so the moat moved away from the code and towards expertise, taste, data and distribution. Second, agents became users of software alongside people: through MCP servers, APIs and command line tools, a program can now have a customer that never opens a window. Third, pricing moved from features to outcomes, closer to how service work is billed.

That third shift is the interesting one. Software has spent two decades charging per seat, which only made sense while a human had to sit in the chair. An agent that books, plans and remembers things does not need a seat. If you cannot explain what outcome the invoice buys, the invoice gets harder to defend.

docs.title: The eight shapes he names
docs.text:
Software-enabled services. Do not sell accounting software, run the accounting firm that is ten times faster. His examples are Crosby and Pilot in accounting, Harvey and EvenUp in legal, Abridge in medical. The pitch is that two people plus AI deliver what a twenty-person firm delivered, and the client buys the finished work rather than a licence.

Vertical agent harnesses. The model is general purpose, so the product is everything around it: the rules, tools, knowledge, workflows and memory. Claude Code is that harness for programming; Ashby expects the same shape to appear in every niche, including very small ones. As models improve, the harness improves with them.

Headless AI software. Tools with no interface at all, built for agents to call. A CLI, an API, an MCP server. His own Eyedropper pulls a design system from a server into whatever project an agent is working on. The obvious risk is the one he names: a model lab can bundle something similar into its next release.

Agent-native systems. A plugin or skill that runs inside the agent the customer already uses, paired with a dashboard that shows progress and collects data. His ProductOS, a free plugin for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, is the example. Coaches and consultants fit here because they already own a repeatable method worth encoding.

Taste-led niche products. Build for the thousand people who already trust you instead of a market of a million. The scarce thing in this category is caring more than anyone else about one narrow subject, and the product does not have to win on features.

Ambient consumer agents. An assistant that lives inside WhatsApp or iMessage instead of asking for an install. Meta's Muse is the current example. The real work is in the interface illusion: the user should never have to understand what an agent is.

Proprietary data products. Anyone can copy your app, nobody can copy your data. Strava's heat maps, Waze traffic, Glassdoor salaries. The test is whether the data is out of distribution for the models, which is another way of asking whether it is worth paying for.

Open-source core. Give the code away and charge for hosting, support, paid tiers and community. PostHog, Supabase and cal.com run this way. The public repository becomes the marketing department.

docs.title: How he would have you choose
docs.text: The mapping is blunt and useful. Service experience or existing clients: type one. Deep niche expertise: vertical harness. One data source or one hard narrow skill: headless. A repeatable method with proof: agent-native system. An audience or a community: taste-led niche product. Ambition for a consumer giant and a tolerance for a brutal market: ambient agent. A body of data nobody else collects: data product. Comfortable building in public: open-source core.

docs.title: Where the argument holds, and where it does not
docs.text:
The three shifts are real. Coding agents did collapse the cost of a CRUD application, and MCP and CLI surfaces did turn agents into genuine users of software. The taxonomy is also more useful than the usual list of AI startup ideas because each type names where the defensibility sits, rather than what the product does.

The weak part is the headline. "Generic SaaS is dying" is a forecast without a measurement behind it: no churn figures, no revenue data, no example of a generic product that failed for the reason he gives. Plenty of unremarkable dashboards still sell, mostly on distribution, integration depth and switching costs, none of which the video counts. A cheap build makes a bad product easier to create, which is not the same as making it impossible to sell.

Two of his own categories carry the risk he mentions in passing. A headless tool can be absorbed by a model lab, and an ambient consumer agent competes with Meta, OpenAI and xAI on the distribution channel those companies own. The taste-led product is deliberately small, which is fine as a business and a poor fit for anyone raising money on growth.

The sharpest observation is buried in the middle: every one of the eight improves as the models improve. That cuts both ways. If your product is a thin layer over a model, the model's next release is your competitor. What survives is the part that is not in the model, which is exactly what he calls the harness, the data, the taste and the audience.

Original video: Stop building SaaS. Build one of these 8 instead.
